Below is one complete Lua solution. Save it (for example as solve.lua), make sure you have an input file called “input.txt” in the same directory, and then run it (e.g. with “lua solve.lua”). This solution reads the grid from input.txt, simulates the beam(s) from the top–left tile (entering from the left so starting with a rightward-moving beam), marks every tile that the light “energizes” (by a beam passing, reflecting, or splitting there) and finally prints the energized‐tile count.

------------------------------------------------------------
-- solve.lua
------------------------------------------------------------
local function readInput(filename)
  local f = io.open(filename, "r")
  if not f then
    error("Could not open " .. filename)
  end
  local grid = {}
  for line in f:lines() do
    table.insert(grid, line)
  end
  f:close()
  return grid
end

-- Reflection for mirrors.
local function reflectMirror(ch, dx, dy)
  -- For mirror '/', the mapping is:
  --   right (0,1)  -> up   (-1,0)
  --   left  (0,-1) -> down (1,0)
  --   down  (1,0)  -> left (0,-1)
  --   up    (-1,0) -> right(0,1)
  --
  -- For mirror '\' the mapping is:
  --   right (0,1)  -> down (1,0)
  --   left  (0,-1) -> up   (-1,0)
  --   down  (1,0)  -> right(0,1)
  --   up    (-1,0) -> left (0,-1)
  if ch == '/' then
    if dx == 0 and dy == 1 then
      return -1, 0
    elseif dx == 0 and dy == -1 then
      return 1, 0
    elseif dx == 1 and dy == 0 then
      return 0, -1
    elseif dx == -1 and dy == 0 then
      return 0, 1
    end
  elseif ch == '\\' then
    if dx == 0 and dy == 1 then
      return 1, 0
    elseif dx == 0 and dy == -1 then
      return -1, 0
    elseif dx == 1 and dy == 0 then
      return 0, 1
    elseif dx == -1 and dy == 0 then
      return 0, -1
    end
  end
  -- If something unexpected then just keep going.
  return dx, dy
end

-- Check if a position is inside the grid.
local function inBounds(r, c, height, width)
  return r >= 1 and r <= height and c >= 1 and c <= width
end

-- Main simulation function.
local function simulate(grid)
  local height = #grid
  local width = #grid[1]

  -- energized[tile_row][tile_col] will be true if energized.
  local energized = {}
  for i = 1, height do
    energized[i] = {}
    for j = 1, width do
      energized[i][j] = false
    end
  end

  -- A state is a beam at position (r,c) with direction (dx,dy).
  local beams = {}         -- queue of beams, each beam is {r, c, dx, dy}
  local queueIndex = 1

  -- Use a set to remember visited states to avoid infinite loops.
  local visited = {}

  -- Helper: make a key string for beam state.
  local function stateKey(r, c, dx, dy)
    return r .. "," .. c .. "," .. dx .. "," .. dy
  end

  -- Enqueue a new beam only if not visited already.
  local function enqueue(r, c, dx, dy)
    local key = stateKey(r, c, dx, dy)
    if not visited[key] then
      table.insert(beams, {r, c, dx, dy})
    end
  end

  -- Starting beam: Top-left tile: row=1, col=1 with direction right (dx=0, dy=1).
  enqueue(1, 1, 0, 1)

  -- Process all beams.
  while queueIndex <= #beams do
    local beam = beams[queueIndex]
    queueIndex = queueIndex + 1
    local r, c, dx, dy = beam[1], beam[2], beam[3], beam[4]
    local key = stateKey(r, c, dx, dy)
    if visited[key] then
      -- Ignore duplicate states.
      goto continue
    end
    visited[key] = true

    -- Mark the current tile as energized.
    if inBounds(r, c, height, width) then
      energized[r][c] = true
    end

    -- Get the current cell type.
    if not inBounds(r, c, height, width) then
      -- Beam is out of bounds.
      goto continue
    end
    local cell = grid[r]:sub(c,c)

    if cell == '.' then
      -- Empty tile. Continue on same path.
      local nr, nc = r + dx, c + dy
      if inBounds(nr, nc, height, width) then
        enqueue(nr, nc, dx, dy)
      end

    elseif cell == '/' or cell == '\\' then
      -- Mirror: reflect beam and go on.
      local ndx, ndy = reflectMirror(cell, dx, dy)
      local nr, nc = r + ndx, c + ndy
      if inBounds(nr, nc, height, width) then
        enqueue(nr, nc, ndx, ndy)
      end

    elseif cell == '|' or cell == '-' then
      -- Splitter.
      -- For a vertical splitter ('|'), the pointy (pass‐through) ends are left/right.
      --   So if the beam is moving horizontally (dx==0) it is pointy => no splitting.
      --   If moving vertically (dy==0) then the beam hits the flat side and splits
      --   into beams going left and right.
      -- For a horizontal splitter ('-'), the pointy ends are up/down.
      --   So if the beam moves vertically (dy==0), it passes through; if horizontally,
      --   then it splits into upward and downward moving beams.
      if cell == '|' then
        if dx == 0 and (dy == 1 or dy == -1) then
          -- Pointy side: pass through unchanged.
          local nr, nc = r + dx, c + dy
          if inBounds(nr, nc, height, width) then
            enqueue(nr, nc, dx, dy)
          end
        else
          -- Flat side: split into two beams: left and right.
          local dirs = {{0, -1}, {0, 1}}
          for _, d in ipairs(dirs) do
            local ndx, ndy = d[1], d[2]
            local nr, nc = r + ndx, c + ndy
            if inBounds(nr, nc, height, width) then
              enqueue(nr, nc, ndx, ndy)
            end
          end
        end
      elseif cell == '-' then
        if dy == 0 and (dx == 1 or dx == -1) then
          -- Pointy side: beam goes straight.
          local nr, nc = r + dx, c + dy
          if inBounds(nr, nc, height, width) then
            enqueue(nr, nc, dx, dy)
          end
        else
          -- Horizontal splitter hit on flat side: split into up and down beams.
          local dirs = {{-1, 0}, {1, 0}}
          for _, d in ipairs(dirs) do
            local ndx, ndy = d[1], d[2]
            local nr, nc = r + ndx, c + ndy
            if inBounds(nr, nc, height, width) then
              enqueue(nr, nc, ndx, ndy)
            end
          end
        end
      end
    end

    ::continue::
  end

  -- Count energized tiles.
  local count = 0
  for r = 1, height do
    for c = 1, width do
      if energized[r][c] then
        count = count + 1
      end
    end
  end
  return count
end

-- Main entry point.
local grid = readInput("input.txt")
local result = simulate(grid)
print(result)

------------------------------------------------------------
-- End of solve.lua
------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation:

1. The program reads your grid file line‐by‐line into a table.
2. It then simulates the beam(s) starting at (1,1) (Lua arrays are 1–indexed) with an initial direction of right.
3. When a beam enters a cell:
   • If the cell is empty (".") it continues in the same direction.
   • If it is a mirror ("/" or "\"), the beam’s direction is changed using the rules in the reflectMirror() function.
   • If it is a splitter ("|" or "-"), the beam’s behavior depends on its direction. For a vertical splitter, a horizontally moving beam simply goes through; a vertically moving beam splits into beams going left and right. For a horizontal splitter, a vertically moving beam goes through; a horizontally moving beam splits into beams going up and down.
4. Every time a beam visits a cell, that cell is “energized”. The program avoids infinite loops by keeping a set of visited states.
5. Finally, the total count of energized cells is printed.

Compile and run this solution with your favorite Lua interpreter. Enjoy solving Advent of Code Day 16!

prompt: Can you write me a Python code that uses `Textualize/textual` library. It must have a button within button. Sol, like I have a list of files and there i can delete the file.
baseline_response:
Below is an example of a small Textual application that displays a list of “file” items. Each file is represented as a composite widget that looks like a button (showing the file name) with an embedded (nested) delete button. When you click on the file’s main button, it logs that you selected the file, and when you click the inner “Delete” button, it logs the deletion and removes the file’s widget from the screen.

Make sure you have Textual installed (pip install textual) before running the code.

------------------------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env python3
from textual.app import App, ComposeResult
from textual.containers import Horizontal
from textual.widgets import Button, Static
from textual import events

class FileItem(Static):
    """
    A composite widget that represents a file.
    It is composed of a “main” button (showing the file name)
    and an inner delete button.
    """
    def __init__(self, file_name: str) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.file_name = file_name

    def compose(self) -> ComposeResult:
        with Horizontal():
            # The file button. (You can click it to “select” the file.)
            yield Button(self.file_name, id="file-btn")
            # The nested delete button.
            yield Button("Delete", id="delete-btn")

    async def on_button_pressed(self, event: Button.Pressed) -> None:
        if event.button.id == "delete-btn":
            # Handle deletion: remove this FileItem widget from its parent.
            self.app.log(f"Deleting file: {self.file_name}")
            await self.remove()
        elif event.button.id == "file-btn":
            # Handle file selection
            self.app.log(f"Selected file: {self.file_name}")

class FileManagerApp(App):
    """A basic file manager TUI app using Textual."""
    CSS = """
    FileItem {
        border: solid darkgray;
        padding: 1 2;
        margin: 1;
    }
    Button {
        margin: 0 1;
    }
    """

    def __init__(self, files: list[str], **kwargs) -> None:
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.files = files

    def compose(self) -> ComposeResult:
        # Create one FileItem widget per file.
        for file in self.files:
            yield FileItem(file)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example list of files
    sample_files = [
        "document1.txt",
        "presentation.pptx",
        "notes.md",
        "image.png",
    ]
    FileManagerApp(sample_files).run()
------------------------------------------------

How the code works:

1. The FileItem widget uses a Horizontal container to place two Button widgets side by side:
   • The first button displays the file name.
   • The second “Delete” button is nested right next to the file button.
   
2. The on_button_pressed handler distinguishes which button was pressed by inspecting event.button.id.
   • On clicking “Delete”, it logs a message and calls await self.remove() to remove the widget.
   • On clicking the file name button, it logs that the file was selected.
   
3. The FileManagerApp instantiates a FileItem for each file in the provided list and runs the app.

Run the code and you’ll see a terminal UI where each file item appears with its own delete button. You can click “Delete” on any file to remove it and click on the file’s name to “select” it (as simulated by logging messages).

This structure demonstrates how you can have a “button within a button” (or more precisely, a composite widget with nested buttons) to manage a list of files with delete functionality using the Textual library.

Setup:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
from pytube import YouTube

def download_audio(url, output_folder="."):
    try:
        # Create YouTube object for the given URL
        yt = YouTube(url)
    except Exception as e:
        print("Error creating YouTube object:", e)
        return

    # Filter out streams that contain only audio
    audio_stream = yt.streams.filter(only_audio=True).first()
    if audio_stream is None:
        print("No audio stream available for this video!")
        return

    try:
        print(f"Downloading: {yt.title}")
        # Download the audio stream.
        downloaded_file = audio_stream.download(output_path=output_folder)
        print("Download complete!")
        
        # Optionally: rename the file extension to '.mp3'
        # Note: This does not convert the file to mp3. For a proper conversion, use a library such as pydub or subprocess with ffmpeg.
        base, ext = os.path.splitext(downloaded_file)
        new_file = base + ".mp3"
        os.rename(downloaded_file, new_file)
        print(f"File saved as: {new_file}")
    except Exception as e:
        print("Error during download:", e)

def main():
    # Ask the user for the YouTube URL and output folder if desired.
    url = input("Enter the YouTube video URL: ").strip()
    if not url:
        print("No URL provided!")
        return

    output_folder = input("Enter the output folder (press Enter for current directory): ").strip()
    if not output_folder:
        output_folder = "."
    elif not os.path.exists(output_folder):
        print("Output folder does not exist. Creating it.")
        os.makedirs(output_folder)

    download_audio(url, output_folder)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

----------------------------------------------------

Notes:
• This script creates a YouTube object from the provided URL using pytube.
• It then filters the streams to select an audio-only stream and downloads it.
• After downloading, the file is renamed to have a .mp3 extension. (Keep in mind that a simple file rename does not perform an actual audio conversion. For converting formats properly, you could use ffmpeg via a Python wrapper like pydub.)
• Always ensure your usage complies with YouTube’s Terms of Service.

candidate_response:
Let's apply the requested meta-cognitive process carefully to solve the problem:

---

### Problem Restatement:
Find the **smallest integer \( x \)** (furthest to the left on the number line) such that:

\[
15 < x^2 < 30
\]

Consider both positive and negative integers.

---

### Step 1: Careful analysis of the problem statement

- We want an integer \( x \).
- The inequality strictly demands \( x^2 \) to be greater than 15 and less than 30.
- The phrase "smallest integer (furthest to the left)" means the integer with the smallest value on the number line, considering negative values as well.
- "Considering both positive and negative integers" explicitly includes negative \( x \).

---

### Step 2: Identify key terms / concepts:

- \( x^2 \) means the square of the integer \( x \).
- \( 15 < x^2 < 30 \): \( x^2 \) strictly between 15 and 30.
- Smallest integer furthest to the left means the minimum integer \( x \).
- The possibility of negative integers matters because \( x^2 \) is nonnegative and symmetric about zero.

---

### Step 3: Consider all possible approaches

A direct approach:

- Find all integers \( x \) with \( 15 < x^2 < 30 \).
- List those integers.
- Pick the "smallest" integer (least number on the number line) from that set.

---

### Step 4: Solve the inequality \( 15 < x^2 < 30 \) for integer \( x \):

- For the inequality:
  
  \[
  15 < x^2 < 30
  \]

- Take square roots (considering \( x \) integer):

  \[
  \sqrt{15} < |x| < \sqrt{30}
  \]

- Numerically:

  - \(\sqrt{15} \approx 3.872\)
  - \(\sqrt{30} \approx 5.477\)

- So,

  \[
  3.872 < |x| < 5.477
  \]

For integers \( x \), possible integer values for \(|x|\) would be \(4\) or \(5\).

- For \( |x| = 4 \):

  \[
  x^2 = 16
  \]

  Check if \( 15 < 16 < 30 \) → **True**

- For \( |x| = 5 \):

  \[
  x^2 = 25
  \]

  Check if \( 15 < 25 < 30 \) → **True**

- For \( |x| = 3 \):

  \[
  3^2 = 9
  \]

  Check if \( 15 < 9 < 30 \) → False (9 not greater than 15)

- For \( |x| = 6 \):

  \[
  6^2 = 36
  \]

  \( 36 > 30 \) → Not satisfying

---

### Step 5: Find all \( x \) such that \( x^2 = 16 \) or \( x^2 = 25 \):

- For \( x^2 = 16 \): \( x = \pm 4 \)
- For \( x^2 = 25 \): \( x = \pm 5 \)

All four values satisfy the inequality \( 15 < x^2 < 30 \).

---

### Step 6: Choose the smallest integer (furthest to the left) among these candidates:

Candidates: \(-5, -4, 4, 5\)

- The smallest (furthest to the left) integer is \(-5\).

---

### Step 7: Verify that \( x = -5 \) satisfies the original condition:

\[
15 < (-5)^2 < 30 \Rightarrow 15 < 25 < 30 \Rightarrow \text{True}
\]

---

### Step 8: Check for edge cases:

- Could \( x = -6 \) or smaller satisfy the inequality? \( (-6)^2 = 36 \not< 30 \)

- Could \( x = -3 \) or larger negative number with lower absolute value satisfy? No, since \( (-3)^2 = 9 \not> 15 \)

No other integers satisfy the inequality and are less than \(-5\).

---

### Step 9: Consider any ambiguities

- "Smallest integer" is unambiguous when considering the number line: the leftmost integer.

- The inequality is strict, so no equality allowed.

- Both positive and negative integers taken into account: confirms \(-5\) is valid.

---

### Final answer:

\[
\boxed{-5}
\]

---

### Summary of reasoning:

- The problem is to find the smallest integer \( x \) such that \( 15 < x^2 < 30 \).

- The integers with squares in this range are \(\pm 4\) and \(\pm 5\).

- Among these, the smallest integer (furthest left on number line) is \(-5\).

- Verification confirms this satisfies the inequality.

Therefore, the **smallest integer \( x \) such that \( 15 < x^2 < 30 \), considering both positive and negative integers, is \(-5\)**.

    Private v0 As Double ' Velocidad inicial del proyectil

        ' Reiniciar la simulación

        time = 0 ' Reiniciar el tiempo de simulación

    End Sub

        ' Calcular la posición del proyectil
        Dim x As Double = v0 * Math.Cos(angle) * time ' Calcular la posición X
        Dim y As Double = buildingHeight + (v0 * Math.Sin(angle) * time) - (0.5 * g * Math.Pow(time, 2)) ' Calcular la posición Y

        ' Actualizar la altura máxima

        ' Dibujar trayectoria completa
        Dim bmp As Bitmap
        If PictureBox1.Image Is Nothing Then

        Else

        End If

        Dim g As Graphics = Graphics.FromImage(bmp) ' Crear un objeto Graphics a partir del Bitmap

        ' Dibujar una línea desde la última posición hasta la posición actual
        If lastX >= 0 AndAlso lastY >= 0 Then
            g.DrawLine(Pens.Red, lastX, lastY, scaledX, scaledY)
        End If

        ' Actualizar la última posición
        lastX = scaledX
        lastY = scaledY

        PictureBox1.Image = bmp ' Actualizar la imagen del PictureBox
    End Sub

    Private Function ValidateInputs() As Boolean
        ' Validar los inputs del usuario
        Dim velocity As Double
        Dim angle As Double
        Dim height As Double
        Dim finalH As Double

        ' Validar que la velocidad inicial sea un número positivo
        If Not Double.TryParse(txtVelocity.Text, velocity) OrElse velocity <= 0 Then

    End Function


    Private Sub CalculateScale()
        ' Calcular el tiempo máximo hasta que el proyectil vuelva a tocar el suelo
        Dim totalTime As Double = (v0 * Math.Sin(angle) + Math.Sqrt(Math.Pow(v0 * Math.Sin(angle), 2) + 2 * g * (buildingHeight - finalHeight))) / g

        ' Calcular la distancia máxima horizontal
        maxX = v0 * Math.Cos(angle) * totalTime

## Ingredients and preparation details:

### 1) White Sponge Cake (x3 layers, 24cm diameter, ~2 cm per layer thickness)

6. Pour batter into frame, smooth.

### 3) Homemade Feuilletine

**Background:** Feuilletine = crispy thin flakes originally from crushed crispy crêpes dentelle.

**How to make:**

You will make very thin crêpe dentelle, bake until crispy, then break into flakes.

**Ingredients:**

- All-purpose flour 40 g
- Granulated sugar 40 g
- Butter, melted 40 g
- Milk 40 g
- Egg white 1 (approx. 30 g)
- Vanilla extract 5 ml
- Pinch of salt

6. Cool completely on rack.

- Whipping cream 300 g
- Sugar 40 g
- Gelatin leaf 3 g (or powder 1 tsp)
- Vanilla extract 5 ml

**Instructions:**

1. Bloom gelatin in cold water.
2. Heat a small amount of purée (~50 g) and dissolve gelatin in it.
3. Mix gelatin purée with remaining purée.
4. Whip cream with sugar to soft peaks.
5. Fold purée mixture gently into whipped cream.
6. Use immediately for layering.

### 7) Whipped cream frosting (for outside and smoothing top)

- Whipping cream (35% fat) 600 g
- Powdered sugar 60 g

In this recipe you’ll make your own crispy feuilletine flakes (don’t just buy them!), prepare three fillings, and bake three sponge‐cake rounds in 26 cm (10‑inch) diameter pans. Read through the recipe completely before beginning.

─────────────────────────────  
1. OVERVIEW & LAYERING  
─────────────────────────────

• You will bake three (≈5 cm–high) white sponge cake rounds using 26 cm round pans.
• You’ll make a light simple syrup to soak the cakes.
• The interior “fillings” are as follows (from bottom upward):
  a) On the bottom cake layer: After soaking, spread a layer of homemade chocolate–hazelnut spread and, over that, scatter a light layer (≈50 g) of homemade feuilletine flakes.
  b) Place the second (middle) sponge cake layer (also soaked) and then spread a generous layer of fruit cream spread (≈500 g total are divided over the cake’s area).
  c) Place the top (third) sponge round, then “glaze” the top by brushing on a thin, uneven covering (≈250 g total) of fruit jelly (we suggest a tangy passion‐fruit jelly for contrast).
• Finally, frost the entire exterior with a light whipped cream frosting. (If desired, you can also gently “curtain” a little extra feuilletine and add some fresh fruit slices on top for garnish.)

─────────────────────────────  
2. INGREDIENTS  
─────────────────────────────

A. White Sponge Cake (3 rounds in 26 cm pans)  
• Large eggs, at room temperature: 10 eggs  
• Granulated sugar: 250 g  
• All‐purpose flour, sifted: 250 g  
• Salt: ¼ tsp  
• Vanilla extract: 1 tsp  
• Unsalted butter, melted and cooled: 100 g  

B. Simple Syrup (for soaking)  
• Granulated sugar: 100 g  
• Water: 100 ml

C. Homemade Chocolate–Hazelnut Spread  
(Blend these until smooth; yield ≈400–450 g)  
• Toasted hazelnuts (skins rubbed off), finely ground: 100 g  
• Milk chocolate (at about 40–45% cocoa content), chopped: 200 g  
• Unsalted butter, melted: 50 g  
• Powdered sugar, sifted: 50 g  
• A pinch of salt

D. Homemade Feuilletine (for crisp “flakes”)  
(You will make a thin, caramelized wafer, then break it by hand into irregular flakes; yield ~150 g)  
• Unsalted butter, melted: 100 g  
• Granulated sugar: 150 g  
• All‐purpose flour: 120 g  
• A pinch of salt  
• (You will spread the mixture very thin–about 2–3 mm–on a 30×40 cm baking sheet.)

E. Fruit Cream Spread (Strawberry Style)  
(You want a smooth, creamy, fruit‐tinted filling; yield ≈500 g)  
• Mascarpone cheese: 250 g  
• Fresh strawberries, pureed and sieved (or high‐quality strawberry puree): 100 g  
• Powdered sugar, sifted: 50 g  
• Heavy cream (30% fat), chilled: 150 g (whipped to soft peaks; see “Whipped Cream” below)  

F. Fruit Jelly (Passion‐Fruit Flavor)  
(Spreadable, not too stiff; yield ≈250 g)  
• Passion‐fruit pulp (from fresh or good quality pulp, strained): 200 g  
• Granulated sugar: 100 g  
• Water: 100 ml  
• Agar agar powder: 3 g  
  Note: (If you prefer gelatin, you could use about 6 g, dissolved in a little water, but agar agar sets more sharply and gives a clear jelly.)  

G. Whipped Cream Frosting  
• Heavy cream (35% fat), chilled: 400 ml  
• Powdered sugar, sifted: 50 g  
• Vanilla extract: 1 tsp

─────────────────────────────  
3. PREPARATIONS  
─────────────────────────────

A. White Sponge Cake  
1. Preheat your oven to 180°C (350°F). Grease three 26 cm round cake pans and line the bottoms with parchment paper.
2. In a large bowl, beat the 10 eggs and 250 g granulated sugar with an electric mixer on high speed for about 8–10 minutes until the mixture becomes tripled in volume and pale.
3. Sift together 250 g flour and ¼ tsp salt. Gently fold the flour into the egg mixture using a spatula. Add the 1 tsp vanilla extract.
4. Gently fold in the melted butter (ensure it is not hot) until just incorporated.
5. Divide the batter evenly among the three pans. Bake for 25–30 minutes or until a skewer inserted in the center comes out clean.
6. Cool the cakes in the pans for 10 minutes, then transfer to a wire rack to cool completely.

B. Simple Syrup  
1. In a small saucepan combine 100 g sugar and 100 ml water. Bring to a boil and let simmer for 2 minutes until the sugar completely dissolves. Remove from heat and let cool to room temperature.

C. Homemade Feuilletine  
1. Preheat your oven to 200°C (392°F). Line a 30×40 cm baking sheet with parchment paper.
2. In a bowl, whisk together 100 g melted unsalted butter, 150 g granulated sugar, 120 g flour, and a pinch of salt until you have a smooth and fairly loose batter.
3. Spread the mixture very thinly (2–3 mm thickness) over the parchment paper.
4. Bake for about 10–12 minutes. Look for a deep golden color and a crispy texture.
5. Remove from the oven and allow to cool completely. Once cool, break the baked wafer into irregular “feuilletine” flakes by hand; you should collect about 150 g of flakes in total.

D. Homemade Chocolate–Hazelnut Spread  
1. In a heatproof bowl, melt the 200 g chopped milk chocolate (you may use a microwave in 20‑second bursts or a double boiler) and then stir in the 50 g melted butter.
2. In a food processor, combine the 100 g toasted hazelnuts, 50 g powdered sugar, and a pinch of salt. Pulse to finely grind (but not to a paste).
3. Add the warm chocolate–butter mixture to the hazelnut powder and blend until smooth. Taste and adjust if needed.
4. (Allow the spread to come to room temperature before using; it should be spreadable.)

E. Fruit Cream Spread  
1. In a medium bowl, mix the 250 g mascarpone with 50 g powdered sugar.
2. Stir in the 100 g strawberry puree gently until blended.
3. In a separate bowl, whip 150 g heavy cream to soft peaks.
4. Fold the whipped cream into the mascarpone mixture very gently until you have a homogenous, airy cream.

F. Fruit Jelly (Passion‐Fruit)  
1. In a small saucepan, combine 100 g granulated sugar and 100 ml water. Bring to a boil.
2. Add 200 g passion‐fruit pulp and 3 g agar agar. Stir continuously and let simmer for about 2 minutes so that the agar agar dissolves thoroughly.
3. Remove from heat and allow the mixture to cool slightly (it will thicken as it cools but must remain spreadable and not firm like a fully set gel). If using gelatin instead, follow the package directions for blooming and dissolving.
   
G. Whipped Cream Frosting  
1. Place 400 ml heavy cream in a chilled bowl. Add 50 g powdered sugar and 1 tsp vanilla extract.
2. Whip until stiff peaks form. (Do not overwhip; the frosting should be light and smooth.)

─────────────────────────────  
4. ASSEMBLY  
─────────────────────────────

Note: If you prefer to assemble the cake a day in advance, wrap it loosely in plastic wrap and chill; let it sit at room temperature about 30 minutes before serving so that the layers soften slightly and the flavors meld.

A. Level each sponge cake if necessary.
B. Using a serrated knife, trim a very thin layer from the top of each cake to create flat surfaces.

C. Assemble in a 26 cm cake stand or large serving platter:

     – Immediately brush the top evenly with about 1/3–1/2 of the simple syrup.
     – Spread the entire surface with the homemade chocolate–hazelnut spread (approximately 300 g total, i.e. about 2/3 of the prepared spread) using an offset spatula.

  2. Gently set the second (middle) sponge cake layer on top.
     – Brush its top with another 1/3–1/2 of the syrup.
     – Spread the fruit cream spread evenly over this second layer (use all or most of the 500 g prepared; smooth out to about a 2–3 cm thickness).
    
  3. Place the top (third) sponge cake layer.
     – Brush the top with the remaining simple syrup.
     – While still slightly warm (or at room temperature), gently “glaze” the top with the passion‐fruit jelly. Use a thin spatula or pastry brush to achieve an uneven, artisanal look using about 250 g of jelly. (If you prefer, you may also let the jelly set into a “mirror‐glaze” style.)
    
  4. Finally, frost the entire exterior (sides and top) with the whipped cream frosting. Use an offset spatula or a piping bag for a neat finish.
     – Optionally, sprinkle a few extra feuilletine flakes (≈50 g) over the top and decorate with fresh strawberry slices (or other complementary fruits) for added color and texture.

─────────────────────────────  
5. NOTES

candidate_response:
Sure! Below is a Kotlin solution for the given problem.

---

### Explanation

We want to minimize the total number of key presses needed to type the word by remapping letters onto keys 2-9. Each key can have multiple letters, and typing the first letter on that key costs 1 press, the second letter costs 2 presses, etc.

---

### Key observations:

- There are 8 keys (2 to 9) to assign letters to.
- Each letter occurs with a certain frequency in the word.
- Given the frequencies of the letters, to minimize the total cost:
  - Assign the highest frequency letters to the "cheapest" positions (i.e., first positions of keys), the next highest frequencies to the second positions, etc.
- The cost to type a letter = (position in the key) * (frequency).
- To minimize cost, sort letters by frequency descending.
- Assign letters to positions 1 through 8 keys, then positions 2 through 8 keys, and so on.

Since keys are unlimited in length, but there are only 8 keys, letter `i` in the sorted list will be assigned position `pos = i / 8 + 1` on some key.

---

### Algorithm:

1. Count frequency of each letter in `word`.
2. Sort frequencies descending.
3. For letter at index `i` in sorted frequencies, compute cost += frequency * (i / 8 + 1)
4. Return total cost.

---

### Code Implementation in Kotlin

```kotlin
fun minimumPresses(word: String): Int {
    // Count frequencies of letters
    val freq = IntArray(26)
    for (ch in word) {
        freq[ch - 'a']++
    }
    
    // Get frequencies > 0 and sort descending
    val sortedFreq = freq.filter { it > 0 }.sortedDescending()
    
    var totalCost = 0
    // For each letter freq, compute minimal presses
    for (i in sortedFreq.indices) {
        val presses = (i / 8) + 1
        totalCost += presses * sortedFreq[i]
    }
    
    return totalCost
}
```

---

### Testing with the examples:

```kotlin
fun main() {
    println(minimumPresses("abcde"))            // Output: 5
    println(minimumPresses("xyzxyzxyzxyz"))     // Output: 12
    println(minimumPresses("aabbccddeeffgghhiiiiii")) // Output: 24
}
```

This matches the expected outputs.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import time
import h5py
import tensorflow as tf

# Define the generator function that yields batches from the HDF5 file
def data_generator(hdf5_file, batch_size):
    with h5py.File(hdf5_file, 'r') as f:
        mfcc_dataset = f['mfcc']
        mel_spectogram_dataset = f['mel_spectrogram']
        label_dataset = f['labels']
        dataset_size = mfcc_dataset.shape[0]

        while True:
            for start_idx in range(0, dataset_size, batch_size):
                end_idx = min(start_idx + batch_size, dataset_size)
                mfcc_batch = mfcc_dataset[start_idx:end_idx]
                mel_spectogram_batch = mel_spectogram_dataset[start_idx:end_idx]
                label_batch = label_dataset[start_idx:end_idx]
                yield (mfcc_batch, mel_spectogram_batch), label_batch

# Function to create a tf.data.Dataset from the generator
def create_tf_dataset(hdf5_file, batch_size):
    output_signature = (
        (tf.TensorSpec(shape=(None, 26, 641), dtype=tf.float32),
         tf.TensorSpec(shape=(None, 160, 641), dtype=tf.float32)),
        tf.TensorSpec(shape=(None,), dtype=tf.int32)
    )
    dataset = tf.data.Dataset.from_generator(
        lambda: data_generator(hdf5_file, batch_size),
        output_signature=output_signature
    )
    # Cache the dataset and prefetch to improve loading speed
    return dataset.cache().prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)

# Benchmarking function to measure batches per second
def benchmark_dataset(dataset, num_batches=100):
    start_time = time.time()
    batch_count = 0

    # Iterate over the dataset to process a fixed number of batches
    for batch in dataset:
        batch_count += 1
        if batch_count >= num_batches:
            break

    end_time = time.time()
    total_time = end_time - start_time
    throughput = num_batches / total_time
    print(f"Processed {num_batches} batches in {total_time:.2f} seconds")
    print(f"Throughput: {throughput:.2f} batches/second")

# Example usage
if __name__ == '__main__':
    hdf5_file = "path_to_your_hdf5_file.hdf5"  # update this with your HDF5 file path
    batch_size = 32  # set your desired batch size
    dataset = create_tf_dataset(hdf5_file, batch_size)
    benchmark_dataset(dataset, num_batches=100)

candidate_response:
The error message:

```
[libopenh264 @ 0x560b8cd94300] Incorrect library version loaded
Error initializing output stream 0:0 -- Error while opening encoder for output stream #0:0 - maybe incorrect parameters such as bit_rate, rate, width or height
```

indicates that ffmpeg is having trouble initializing the video encoder, specifically related to the `libopenh264` library. This is a common issue when there's a version mismatch or an incompatibility in the installed codecs or ffmpeg build.

Here's how you can resolve it:

---

### 1. Verify FFmpeg Installation and Version

Check which ffmpeg is being used and its version:

```bash
which ffmpeg
ffmpeg -version
```

If you're on Linux or macOS, ensure it's a recent build from a reliable source.

---

### 2. Reinstall or Update FFmpeg

If ffmpeg is outdated or installed with broken codecs, reinstall or update it.

- **On Ubuntu/Debian:**

```bash
sudo apt remove ffmpeg
sudo apt update
sudo apt install ffmpeg
```

Or install the latest via a PPA (more up-to-date):

```bash
sudo add-apt-repository ppa:savoury1/ffmpeg4
sudo apt update
sudo apt install ffmpeg
```

- **On macOS (using Homebrew):**

```bash
brew reinstall ffmpeg
```

You may want to install ffmpeg with all codecs enabled:

```bash
brew install ffmpeg --with-libopenh264 --with-libvpx --with-libx264
```

---

### 3. Avoid Using `libopenh264`

Since the error is related to `libopenh264`, try using a different encoder like `libx264`.

Matplotlib animation's `ani.save()` lets you specify the codec with `extra_args`.

Example:

```python
ani.save('animation.mp4', writer='ffmpeg', dpi=200, 
         extra_args=['-vcodec', 'libx264'])
```

You can also specify the bitrate or other params:

```python
ani.save('animation.mp4', writer='ffmpeg', dpi=200, 
         extra_args=['-vcodec', 'libx264', '-crf', '23', '-preset', 'medium'])
```

---

### 4. Check the Animation Resolution

Sometimes the resolution isn't a multiple of 2, causing encoding errors.

Ensure your figure and output video size have even width and height.

Example, set the figure size before saving:

```python
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6,4))  # width and height in inches
# your plotting code...
```

Try to keep width * dpi and height * dpi as even numbers (e.g., 1200x800).

---

### 5. Try Saving Using a Different Codec or Format

If `.mp4` with `ffmpeg` and `libopenh264` fails, try saving as `.gif` or `.avi` to isolate the issue.

Example saving as GIF:

```python
ani.save('animation.gif', writer='pillow')
```

---

### Summary and Example of a Working Saving Command:

```python
ani.save('animation.mp4', writer='ffmpeg', dpi=200,
         extra_args=['-vcodec', 'libx264', '-pix_fmt', 'yuv420p'])
```

Make sure:

- ffmpeg is correctly installed and updated
- your figure resolution is valid
- you specify codec as `libx264` and pixel format as `yuv420p`

This kind of error usually means that ffmpeg is loading a version of the libopenh264 library that it doesn’t expect. In other words, there’s a version or compatibility mismatch between ffmpeg (or its codec configuration) and the installed libopenh264. Here are some steps you can take to resolve the issue:

1. Verify Your ffmpeg Installation

  • Check which ffmpeg you’re using (the one invoked in your Jupyter environment) by running in a terminal:
   ffmpeg -version

  • Verify that the reported version and configuration match your expectations. Sometimes multiple installations (e.g., one installed via conda and another via the system package manager) can lead to these issues.

2. Update or Reinstall ffmpeg and Dependencies

  • The error “Incorrect library version loaded” comes from libopenh264. If you installed ffmpeg via a package manager (like apt, Homebrew, or conda), try updating it:
   For Conda (if you’re using it), you can run:
    conda update -c conda-forge ffmpeg

  • Alternatively, uninstall and reinstall ffmpeg so that it properly links with the expected version of libopenh264.

3. Try Specifying a Different Codec

  • Sometimes it’s easier to work around the issue by choosing a different codec that doesn’t rely on that exact library version. For example, you can use the popular libx264 codec by modifying your save call:
   ani.save('animation.mp4', writer='ffmpeg', codec='libx264', extra_args=['-pix_fmt', 'yuv420p'], dpi=200)
  • The extra_args option forces a pixel format that is widely compatible and might sidestep issues.

4. Consistency in the Environment

  • If you installed ffmpeg from different sources (e.g., one via apt and one via conda), conflicts can arise. Try making sure that your entire environment comes from one source (using conda packages for both Python packages and ffmpeg is one good strategy).

5. Check Your OS-Specific Libraries

  • On some systems the ffmpeg build might be linked to a system version of libopenh264 that has been updated separately. You might have to force a reinstall or downgrade of libopenh264 so that it is consistent with the build expectation of your ffmpeg.
  • For instance, on Ubuntu you might try:
   sudo apt-get update
   sudo apt-get install --reinstall libopenh264-5
   (Replace “libopenh264-5” with the appropriate package version for your system.)

6. Rebuild ffmpeg (Advanced)

  • If you built ffmpeg from source, try recompiling ffmpeg so that it can correctly detect and link against your installed version of libopenh264.

By following one or more of these strategies, you should be able to resolve the mismatch that’s causing the animation saving process to fail. Often the simplest solution is to update/align your ffmpeg installation and/or switch to a different codec in your ani.save() call.

Hopefully, one of these suggestions helps you get your animation saved without that error!

Certainly! To make solid magnesium become liquid (i.e., melt it), you need to supply enough heat to reach its melting point. Magnesium has a melting point of about **650 °C**. One way to do this is via a combustion reaction that produces enough heat to melt the solid magnesium.

### Objective
To demonstrate the melting of solid magnesium by using a combustion reaction to supply heat.

---

## Laboratory Experiment: Melting Solid Magnesium via Combustion Reaction

### Materials
- Magnesium ribbon (about 5 cm length)
- Bunsen burner (or a propane torch)
- Crucible (heat-resistant ceramic or metal crucible)
- Tongs or crucible holder
- Heat-resistant gloves
- Safety goggles
- Lab coat
- Fireproof surface or lab bench with protective mat
- Metal tweezers or forceps
- Stopwatch or timer (optional)

### Background
Magnesium is a reactive metal that burns with a bright white flame when ignited in air, which produces magnesium oxide and releases a significant amount of heat:

\[
2 \text{Mg (s)} + \text{O}_2 \text{(g)} \rightarrow 2 \text{MgO (s)} + \text{heat}
\]

The heat from burning magnesium can melt excess magnesium placed nearby (or in direct contact in a crucible).

---

### Safety Precautions
- Magnesium burns very brightly and intensely; avoid looking directly at the flame to protect your eyes.
- Wear safety goggles and a lab coat.
- Handle hot equipment with tongs and gloves.
- Work in a well-ventilated lab or under a fume hood.
- Have a fire extinguisher or sand bucket nearby.

---

### Procedure

1. **Preparation**
   - Put on your safety goggles, lab coat, and gloves.
   - Place the crucible on a fireproof surface.
   - Coil the magnesium ribbon loosely and place it in the crucible.

2. **Heating**
   - Using the Bunsen burner, light the magnesium ribbon from the edges.
   - The magnesium will begin to burn with a bright white flame.
   - As it burns, observe the heat generated inside the crucible.

3. **Melting Observation**
   - As the combustion proceeds, the heat released may be enough to melt a portion of the magnesium ribbon.
   - Observe the physical state of the magnesium in the crucible; you may notice some molten (liquid) magnesium forming or droplets of liquid metal.

4. **Cooling**
   - After burning for several seconds (or once the magnesium is consumed), turn off the flame, and allow the crucible to cool under observation.
   - Do **not** touch the crucible until it has cooled thoroughly.

5. **Post-experiment analysis**
   - Examine the crucible contents: you should notice solid magnesium oxide and possibly solidified droplets of magnesium metal which was molten.
   - Discuss the reaction and heat energy transfer that caused solid magnesium to melt.

---

### Explanation
In this experiment, the combustion reaction of magnesium in oxygen produces enough heat to increase the temperature of the magnesium metal itself above its melting point, causing it to liquefy temporarily. This demonstrates a chemical method of melting magnesium via exothermic reaction.

---

### Notes
- Heating pure magnesium metal with a Bunsen burner flame alone (without combustion) is typically not enough to melt it due to the melting point being quite high (~650°C) and Bunsen burner temperatures reaching around 1100°C but heat loss makes it difficult.
- The oxidizing combustion reaction releases sufficient heat to melt the magnesium locally.
- Direct electric heating (with a crucible furnace) is another common method to melt magnesium.

---

Note: There isn’t a chemical “reaction” that simply changes solid magnesium (Mg) into liquid magnesium while leaving it as elemental magnesium. Most reactions involving magnesium convert it into a compound (for example, burning magnesium in oxygen produces magnesium oxide). In contrast, the process of melting magnesium is a physical phase change that occurs when it is heated above its melting point (about 650°C). 

That said, if your goal is to observe magnesium in its liquid state, you can design an experiment that supplies the required energy to melt solid magnesium. Below is an example of a full laboratory experiment designed to melt magnesium—not via a chemical reaction with another reagent, but by controlled heating in an inert atmosphere to prevent unwanted oxidation.

──────────────────────────────
Title: Melting Magnesium in an Inert Atmosphere

Objective:
• To melt solid magnesium (Mg) by applying thermal energy and to observe the phase change from solid to liquid.
• To practice high-temperature handling techniques and inert-atmosphere procedures for reactive metals.

Background:
Magnesium has a melting point of approximately 650°C. When heated in ambient air, magnesium may rapidly oxidize or even ignite. To safely melt magnesium without altering its chemical composition, it is necessary to perform the experiment under an inert gas (such as argon) and use equipment that can reliably achieve and maintain high temperatures. This experiment is a physical process (phase change) rather than a chemical reaction.

Materials and Apparatus:
• High-purity solid magnesium sample (purity >99.9%; shape: small ingot or button)
• High-temperature induction or resistance furnace capable of reaching at least 800°C
• Graphite or high-alumina (refractory) crucible (compatible with molten magnesium)
• Inert gas supply (argon cylinders with proper regulators)
• Inert-atmosphere glovebox or sealed high-temperature chamber (if available)
• Thermocouple and temperature controller for precise temperature monitoring
• Protective mold (made of a refractory material) for casting the molten magnesium (optional)
• Personal protective equipment (PPE): heat-resistant gloves, face shield, lab coat, safety goggles
• Fire suppression equipment rated for metal fires (Class D extinguisher)
• Tools for transferring and handling hot materials (tongs, crucible lifter)

Procedure:
1. Preparation and Safety Checks:
   a. Review the safety data for magnesium and ensure that all personnel are familiar with the hazards of working with reactive metals at high temperatures.
   b. Ensure the furnace is in a well-ventilated area and that the inert gas (argon) supply is operational.
   c. Prepare the crucible by cleaning it thoroughly and preheating it slightly if recommended by your furnace’s guidelines.
   d. Set up the thermocouple and connect it to the temperature controller to continuously monitor the crucible temperature.

2. Inert Atmosphere Setup:
   a. If using a glovebox or sealed chamber, purge the chamber with argon gas until the oxygen level is negligible.
   b. Alternatively, if the furnace is equipped with an inert-atmosphere option, follow the manufacturer’s instructions for purging air with argon.
 
3. Loading the Sample:
   a. Using appropriate tongs and under the inert atmosphere, place the magnesium sample carefully into the crucible.
   b. Ensure the sample is isolated from any contaminants (such as moisture or oxygen).

4. Heating:
   a. Insert the loaded crucible into the furnace.
   b. Begin heating gradually. Increase the temperature at a controlled rate (e.g., 50°C per minute) to minimize thermal shock.
   c. Monitor the temperature closely. Once the temperature reaches about 650°C, observe the magnesium for signs of melting. (At this point, you may notice a change in the appearance as the metal transitions from solid to liquid.)
   d. Hold the temperature at approximately 700°C for several minutes to ensure complete melting.

5. Observation and Data Collection:
   a. Record the time required to reach the melting point.
   b. Document any observations regarding the appearance and behavior of the magnesium as it melts.
   c. Inquire whether the molten magnesium remains stable in the crucible under the inert atmosphere.

6. Casting (Optional):
   a. If desired, once fully molten, you can carefully pour the magnesium into a preheated refractory mold. (Note: Pouring molten magnesium must be done with extreme caution, as it is still highly reactive and remains at very high temperatures.)
   b. Allow the mold to cool under an inert atmosphere if possible, then observe the solidified magnesium.

7. Cooling and Cleanup:
   a. Turn off the furnace and allow the system to cool to a safe handling temperature before processing further.
   b. Once cooled, remove the crucible and any casted magnesium remnants.
   c. Dispose of or store all materials according to your laboratory’s safety protocols.

8. Post-Experiment Discussion:
   a. Discuss the importance of maintaining an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation or combustion.
   b. Compare the theoretical melting point with the observed behavior.
   c. Reflect on the challenges and safety considerations inherent in working with highly reactive, low-melting-point metals.

Safety Considerations:
• Magnesium is highly reactive, particularly when molten. Ensure that all experiments are conducted in a controlled environment with proper inert atmosphere precautions.
• Never expose molten magnesium to ambient air or moisture.
• Follow all institutional guidelines regarding the handling of high-temperature materials and reactive metals.
• Keep a fire extinguisher rated for metal fires (Class D) in the vicinity.
• Dispose of any waste materials according to appropriate hazardous waste procedures.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion:
This experiment demonstrates that obtaining liquid magnesium from its solid form is achieved via a high-temperature melting process. It is not accomplished through a chemical reaction that simply "transforms" solid magnesium into its liquid state, because any chemical reaction would typically alter the element into a compound. Instead, precise thermal management and an inert atmosphere allow you to observe the phase change of magnesium while maintaining it in its metallic state.

By following this procedure, you can safely study the melting behavior of magnesium, gaining practical experience in high-temperature operations and the critical importance of controlled atmospheres when working with reactive metals.

──────────────────────────────
Additional Notes:
• Always consult with a qualified laboratory supervisor before performing high-temperature experiments.
• Ensure all safety protocols are met, as working with molten metals carries significant risks.
• Although it might be tempting to use an exothermic reaction to generate the needed heat, note that reactions like magnesium combusting in air will form magnesium oxide rather than leaving you with liquid magnesium.

This experiment offers a controlled method to achieve the desired phase change without altering the chemical identity of magnesium.

### Context

The question refers to **five specific tools for improving the new product development (NPD) process** identified in the textbook (note: your question mentions "six tools," but the book in Chapter 11 identifies five main tools for improving the NPD process). These tools are designed to enhance the efficiency, creativity, and success rate of new product development, but each has trade-offs and is better suited for certain technological innovation contexts.

## 1. Stage-Gate Process

**Description:**  
A structured process that divides the NPD into stages separated by gates—decision points where continuation, modification, or termination is decided based on specific criteria.

**Advantages:**  
- Provides discipline, reduces risk by early detection of problems  
- Ensures resources are committed only if criteria are met  
- Increases project visibility and accountability

**Disadvantages:**  
- Can slow down development due to bureaucracy  
- May stifle creativity if too rigid

**Recommendation:**

**Description:**

**Advantages:**

- Improves communication among functions, reducing delays and misalignments

**Disadvantages:**  
- Potential for conflict due to differing priorities  
- Coordination challenges

**Recommendation:**  
**Strongly Use** — Establish multidisciplinary teams early and maintain them across NPD stages for continuous collaboration and knowledge sharing.

---

## 3. Simultaneous or Concurrent Engineering

**Description:**  
Parallelization of development activities (e.g., designing hardware and software simultaneously rather than sequentially).

**Advantages:**  
- Reduces development time significantly  
- Improves integration by early identification of interface issues  
- Enables faster response to market changes

**Disadvantages:**  
- Requires strong coordination and communication  
- Risk of costly rework if assumptions during parallel tasks are wrong

**Recommendation:**  
**Use with strong project management** — Implement concurrent engineering but invest in robust communication platforms and project management tools to minimize risks.

---

## 4. Platform Technologies

**Description:**  
Using common technological components or architectures as foundations for multiple products.

**Advantages:**  
- Reduces development cost and time by reusing components  
- Increases standardization and product consistency  
- Facilitates faster scaling of new products

**Disadvantages:**  
- Limits product differentiation  
- May restrict innovation if platform is inflexible  
- Risk of obsolescence if platform is outdated

**Evaluation for Proposed Innovation:**  
If the company already has a sensor technology or AI algorithm platform, reusing it accelerates development. But for a novel disease detection algorithm or sensor, a new platform may be required initially.

**Recommendation:**  
**Selective use** — Leverage existing platform technologies where appropriate (e.g., sensor hardware), but allow new developments for core AI algorithms needing innovation.

## 5. Open Innovation

**Description:**  
Incorporating external ideas, knowledge, and technologies by collaborating with universities, startups, or crowdsourcing.

- Access to diverse expertise and technologies

### Final remarks

Selecting these tools depends on the specific characteristics of the innovation, the firm's capabilities, time urgency, and market dynamics. In the discussion that follows, assume that your final project is a Smart Home Energy Management System (SHEMS) that integrates IoT devices, data analytics, and user‐friendly control interfaces to optimize household energy consumption. (Any technologically innovative product could be substituted, but this example illustrates the process.) Each tool is analyzed with reference to its advantages, disadvantages, and its likely fit with the development challenges of SHEMS.

────────────────────────────
1. Stage–Gate Process

Advantages:
 • Provides a formal, milestone‐based structure that enables systematic review and decision‐making.
 • Helps in risk management by requiring evaluation at each “gate” and by ensuring that a product concept meets key criteria before moving forward.
 • Offers solid documentation and transparency that can be helpful for large, interdisciplinary projects.

Disadvantages:
 • The process can be relatively rigid and sequential. As a result, it may slow down iterations in an environment where fast feedback is valuable.
 • Rigid stage boundaries may not reflect the emergent, often iterative insights coming from user testing or rapid technological change.

Recommendation for SHEMS:
For a technologically complex product like the SHEMS—where hardware integration, software development, and customer requirements converge—a stage–gate process can offer structure and risk control. However, because such innovations benefit from agility, it is advisable to use a modified or “lean” gate process that allows some iteration within stages. Overall, the stage–gate process should be used, but with flexibility built in for rapid feedback and iteration.

────────────────────────────
2. Concurrent Engineering

Advantages:
 • Encourages simultaneous development across different functions (hardware, software, manufacturing, user design), which can reduce overall time-to-market.
 • Boosts communication among diverse teams, thereby reducing integration problems later in the process.
 • Supports early identification of potential design conflicts and facilitates cross-functional problem solving.

Disadvantages:
 • Requires a high level of coordination and communication; misalignment among teams can lead to confusion or delays.
 • In fast-evolving technologies, aligning simultaneous inputs may prove challenging if team members are not well trained in cross-functional collaboration.

Recommendation for SHEMS:
The SHEMS integrates several elements—from sensors and controllers to data analytics and user interfaces—and thus faces considerable integration challenges. Concurrent engineering will encourage the necessary collaboration and expedite development. Provided that clear communication protocols and collaborative tools are in place, this tool is well suited to the project.

────────────────────────────
3. Quality Function Deployment (QFD)

Advantages:
 • Systematically translates customer and market needs into technical requirements, ensuring that the product features align with user priorities.
 • Provides a structured approach (often using “House of Quality”) to prioritize features based on consumer demand and competitive factors.
 • Improves cross-functional understanding of market needs.

Disadvantages:
 • QFD can be time-consuming and resource intensive, potentially slowing early-stage development if over-applied.
 • Overemphasis on current customer needs runs the risk of stifling breakthrough, disruptive features if not balanced with a technology push perspective.

Recommendation for SHEMS:
Since the success of the SHEMS depends critically on understanding diverse consumer energy concerns and preferences, QFD is a valuable tool for ensuring that the system’s functionalities (such as automated energy controls, real-time monitoring, and predictive analytics) map well onto what users value. Use QFD especially in the concept definition and early design stages—but maintain balance by allowing room for innovative features that may not arise directly from initial customer input.

────────────────────────────
4. Prototyping and Rapid Prototyping Tools

Advantages:
 • Allows teams to develop initial versions of hardware components, software interfaces, and integrated systems to obtain early feedback.
 • Helps in identifying design flaws and usability issues well before full-scale production.
 • Supports iterative learning and agile adaptation based on user responses and technical testing.

Disadvantages:
 • Early prototypes may be incomplete or not fully representative of the final product, which can lead to misinterpretations if customer testing is not carefully managed.
 • Rapid prototyping tools may require additional investment in both time and technology that might not be fully optimized for all types of product features.

Recommendation for SHEMS:
Given that the SHEMS combines tangible hardware with sophisticated software, building prototypes is essential to test system integration, user interfaces, and IoT communications early in the process. Rapid prototyping should be used to enable iterative refinements and validate technical feasibility. It is a highly recommended tool for this kind of innovation.

────────────────────────────
5. Design for Manufacturability (DFM)

Advantages:
 • Ensures that product design is aligned with efficient, cost-effective manufacturing processes.
 • Can reduce production costs and improve quality by identifying potential manufacturing issues during the design phase.
 • Increases the scalability of production, which is critical for achieving cost advantages and meeting market demand.

Disadvantages:
 • An intense focus on manufacturability may constrain creative design options or lead to compromises in functionality or aesthetics.
 • Requires early collaboration with manufacturing experts, which can complicate the design process especially in a start-up or research-driven environment.

Recommendation for SHEMS:
The SHEMS is likely to involve custom hardware such as embedded sensors and controllers, meaning that early attention to production issues is warranted. DFM is critical to ensure that once the product design is stabilized, scale-up for mass production does not lead to unexpected cost or quality issues. Use DFM, especially in parallel with prototyping and final design phases, to balance innovation with manufacturability.

────────────────────────────
6. Agile/Lean Product Development Methods

(Although some texts describe five improvement tools, the textbook also discusses elements related to agile and lean methodologies as critical for expediting innovation. Here we treat agile/lean as the sixth tool.)

Advantages:
 • Emphasizes iterative development, continuous feedback, and flexible planning—an ideal match for software development and rapid market changes.
 • Enhances responsiveness to customer feedback and evolving market conditions.
 • Often results in more adaptable project management and can accelerate time-to-market.

Disadvantages:
 • Agile and lean methods, while flexible, can sometimes lead to less formal documentation or structure, which might be problematic in projects requiring stringent regulatory compliance or coordination with manufacturing.
 • A continually evolving scope may introduce integration challenges with more rigid components (e.g., hardware manufacturing processes).

Recommendation for SHEMS:
Because the SHEMS involves significant software components and must adapt quickly to feedback from early user testing, an agile development approach is particularly valuable. Elements of lean product development can also help minimize waste, streamline development practices, and focus resources on high-value work. It is advisable to adopt agile practices for the software and user interface components while ensuring that coordination with hardware design (which might follow more structured stage–gate or DFM approaches) is maintained.

────────────────────────────
Summary

For your Smart Home Energy Management System, the recommended approach is to combine structure and discipline with flexibility:

• Use a modified stage–gate process to structure the overall development while allowing iteration.
• Employ concurrent engineering to foster cross-functional collaboration among hardware, software, and systems teams.
• Apply QFD early on to align product features with customer needs without losing sight of innovative opportunities.
• Utilize rapid prototyping to iteratively test and refine product components.
• Integrate DFM principles as the design nears stabilization to ensure smooth and cost-effective scaling for production.
• Embed agile/lean methods within the software and interface development cycles to rapidly respond to user feedback and evolving requirements.

By tailoring each tool to the specific challenges and features of your SHEMS innovation, you can build an NPD process that is both disciplined and responsive—a dual imperative for managing technological innovation successfully.
