      # so in the derivation output we assume something like: )
      cp -r theme-tmp/deluge/ui/web/icons \
           $out/lib/python3.8/site-packages/deluge/ui/web/
      cp -r theme-tmp/deluge/ui/web/images \
           $out/lib/python3.8/site-packages/deluge/ui/web/
      
      # Edit index.html: insert the meta viewport tag in the <head>.
      # (Here we assume that <head> appears on one line.
      # You might need to adjust the matching pattern.)
      substituteInPlace $out/lib/python3.8/site-packages/deluge/ui/web/index.html \
         --replace "<head>" "<head>\n  <meta name=\"viewport\" content=\"width=device-width, initial-scale=1, minimum-scale=1, maximum-scale=1\">"
    ''
  });
}
------------------------------------------------------------

Notes:

• We use wget and tar inside postFixup. (If you prefer, you can also use pkgs.fetchurl or pkgs.fetchTarball—but then you have to “copy” its files in the build phase.)
• Adjust “lib/python3.8/site-packages/…” to the correct location in your deluge package output.
• If your deluge derivation is in a different attribute (for example under “python3.pkgs.deluge”), then modify the overlay accordingly.

Step 2. Tell Nix about your overlay

You can add the overlay to your configuration by one of the usual methods. For example, if you manage your overlays via your “~/.config/nixpkgs/overlays” folder, simply put the above file there (or include it in your “default.nix” overlays list). Alternatively, if you’re using NixOS system overlays, add a reference in your /etc/nixos/configuration.nix like:

------------------------------------------------------------
{ pkgs, ... }:
{
  nixpkgs.overlays = [ (import ~/my-overlays/deluge-dark-theme.nix) ];
  # … your other configuration settings …
}
------------------------------------------------------------

Then rebuild your system (nixos-rebuild switch) or update your user profile.

Step 3. Configure deluge’s web.conf

Unlike files in /nix/store you still want to set user‑overridable config. (In your original instructions you modified web.conf.) On NixOS the web UI configuration (for deluge‑web) is typically stored under your user’s~/.config/deluge/ or under the deluge daemon’s configuration directory. You can modify that file manually or via a home-manager module if you’re using home-manager.

For example, create or edit ~/.config/deluge/web.conf so that the theme line reads:

------------------------------------------------------------
{
  ...,
  "theme": "dark"
}
------------------------------------------------------------

Be sure that if you see a backup file (like web.conf~) you update or remove it.

Step 4. Restart deluge‑web

Once rebuilt and installed, restart deluge‑web. (On NixOS you might be running deluge as a service so use “systemctl restart deluge-web.service” or similar.)

────────────────────────────
Why this works

• Since the /nix/store is immutable, you must “patch” a package at build time. Overlays are the Nix way to modify or extend packages.
• The postFixup hook runs after the main installation process but before the derivation is finalized—letting you add extra files (like the dark theme’s icons and images) and tweak bundled files (like index.html).

────────────────────────────
Customizing further

You might want to have more fine‑grained control. For example, if the positioning of the meta tag in index.html changes you could use a different substituteInPlace pattern or even patch the file with a patch file stored in your repository. The general approach remains the same: override the package so that once built it already matches your desired theme configuration.

────────────────────────────
Summary

In NixOS you don’t modify files in /nix/store manually. Instead you override the deluge package derivation with an overlay that, in its build phases, fetches and extracts the dark theme tarball, copies the icons and images into the proper place, and uses substituteInPlace to patch index.html. Your user configuration (web.conf) remains separate and can be updated as usual.

This “everything in Nix” approach means you can reproduce your system configuration on any machine and you don’t have to worry about the store being read‑only.

Happy hacking!

prompt: Act as a Senior Drupal 9 Developer and craft an entity query to display a teaser list of article nodes that share the taxonomy tag 'foobar'. Ensure that the entity query is efficient and performs optimally. Additionally, incorporate basic Bootstrap 5 styles for rendering the list of nodes. Be sure to follow Drupal 9 coding standards and best practices throughout.

To start with, our own perceptual treatment of colorfulness involves the difference between Red and Green and the difference between Blue and Yellow:

a ~ R-G
b ~ B - (R + G)/2

or something like that

but the process above suggests a more symmetrical and three-dimensional notion of colorfulness that isn’t grounded in perception:

a’ ~ R - (G + B)
b’ ~ G - (R + B)
c’ ~ B - (R + G)

so my question really was more, how would you take such a more perceptually grounded version with only two dimensions and map it over these three dimensions to get the “perceptual equivalent” of what the math tells us for this infinite saturation compression limit.
candidate_response:
Great question! You’re touching on a classic and deep problem in color science: how to reconcile the dimensionality and structure of **perceptually grounded color opponent channels** with a more **mathematically symmetric representation** that arises from purely algebraic manipulation of the RGB space.

---

### Background

- The standard opponent color channels, often used in color vision research, map RGB into two key chromatic axes:

  \[
  a \sim R - G
  \]
  \[
  b \sim B - \frac{R + G}{2}
  \]

  These \( a, b \) axes correspond perceptually to our experience of **reddish-greenish** and **bluish-yellowish** contrasts.  

- Your suggested symmetrical 3D mapping:

  \[
  a' \sim R - (G + B)
  \]
  \[
  b' \sim G - (R + B)
  \]
  \[
  c' \sim B - (R + G)
  \]

  is mathematically appealing and symmetrical but results in three opponent-like channels rather than the two perceptual ones.

---

### The Question Restated:

How can one **project or reconcile** this 3D symmetric vector \((a', b', c')\) from RGB onto the **perceptually grounded 2D opponent space** \((a,b)\)?

---

## Step 1: Visualize the symmetric 3D space

The vectors \((a', b', c')\) make use of the difference between one primary channel and the **sum** of the other two channels:

\[
a' = R - (G+B), \quad b' = G - (R+B), \quad c' = B - (R+G)
\]

Note:

- These satisfy \(a' + b' + c' = 0\). This means \(\mathbf{v} = (a', b', c')\) lies **in a 2D subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^3\)** defined by:

\[
a' + b' + c' = 0
\]

Hence, the space is actually **2D**, but embedded in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

---

## Step 2: Recognize the 2D opponent subspace within the 3D symmetric space

- Since \(a' + b' + c' = 0\), the vector \(\mathbf{v}\) is constrained to the plane:

\[
\{ (x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid x + y + z = 0 \}
\]

This plane has dimension 2.

- The classical opponent channels are **different bases of this same 2D plane**.

---

## Step 3: Express classical opponent axes \((a,b)\) as linear combinations of \((a', b', c')\)

Let’s write the classical opponent axes more explicitly in terms of \((a', b', c')\).

Recall:

\[
a = R - G
\]
\[
b = B - \frac{R + G}{2}
\]

Express \(R, G, B\) in terms of \(a', b', c'\):

Given the definitions:

\[
a' = R - (G + B)
\]
\[
b' = G - (R + B)
\]
\[
c' = B - (R + G)
\]

We want to solve for \(R, G, B\) in terms of \(a', b', c'\).

1. Sum all three equations:

\[
a' + b' + c' = R - (G + B) + G - (R + B) + B - (R + G) = 0
\]

(As expected.)

2. Rearrange to isolate \(R, G, B\):

Rewrite the system as:

\[
a' = R - G - B
\]
\[
b' = G - R - B
\]
\[
c' = B - R - G
\]

Sum gives:

\[
a' + b' + c' = (R - G - B) + (G - R - B) + (B - R - G) = - (R + G + B)
\]

But the earlier step shows it sums to 0, so this form suggests a sign issue. Actually, from your initial definitions:

\[
a' = R - (G + B)
\]
\[
b' = G - (R + B)
\]
\[
c' = B - (R + G)
\]

Sum \(= (R + G + B) - 2(R + G + B) = - (R + G + B)\).

For sum = 0, the input RGB values must satisfy \(R + G + B = 0\), impossible for positive colors.

Hence likely you meant:

\[
a' = 2R - (G + B)
\]
\[
b' = 2G - (R + B)
\]
\[
c' = 2B - (R + G)
\]

This is a common symmetrical opponent definition, emphasizing the target channel twice minus the other two.

---

### Using the symmetric formula:

\[
a' = 2R - (G + B)
\]
\[
b' = 2G - (R + B)
\]
\[
c' = 2B - (R + G)
\]

Sum is:

\[
a' + b' + c' = 2(R + G + B) - 2(R + G + B) = 0
\]

Perfect.

---

## Step 4: Express classical opponent channels in terms of these

Given this choice, the classical opponent axis \(a = R - G\) and \(b = B - (R + G)/2\) can be formulated as:

\[
a = R - G = \frac{1}{3} (a' - b')
\]
\[
b = B - \frac{R + G}{2} = \frac{1}{3} \left( -\frac{a' + b'}{2} + c' \right)
\]

This comes from rearranging the equations:

- From the symmetric definitions:

\[
a' = 2R - (G + B)
\]
\[
b' = 2G - (R + B)
\]
\[
c' = 2B - (R + G)
\]

Sum \(a' + b' + c' = 0\).

Consider now the vector mapping:

\[
(a,b) = M (a', b', c')
\]

where \(M\) is a \(2 \times 3\) matrix to be determined.

---

Specifically:

- For \(a = R - G\), use:

\[
R = \frac{a' + b' + 2c'}{3} + ... \quad \text{(found by solving)}, 
\]

but simpler is to invert the symmetric system.

---

**Solving for \(R,G,B\):**

From \(a', b', c'\):

\[
a' = 2R - (G + B)
\]
\[
b' = 2G - (R + B)
\]
\[
c' = 2B - (R + G)
\]

Add:

\[
a' + b' + c' = 0
\]

Add first two equations:

\[
a' + b' = 2R - (G + B) + 2G - (R + B) = (2R - G - B) + (2G - R - B) = (2R - G - B + 2G - R - B) = (R + G - 2B)
\]

Similarly, subtract \(a' - b'\):

\[
a' - b' = (2R - (G + B)) - (2G - (R + B)) = 2R - G - B - 2G + R + B = 3R - 3G
\]

Therefore:

\[
a' - b' = 3 (R - G) \implies R - G = \frac{a' - b'}{3} = a
\]

That matches the classical opposing axis for red-green **exactly**.

---

Similarly for blue-yellow \(b\):

Recall:

\[
b = B - \frac{R + G}{2}
\]

Also,

\[
c' = 2B - (R + G)
\]

So,

\[
b = B - \frac{R + G}{2} = \frac{2B - (R + G)}{2} = \frac{c'}{2}
\]

**Thus:**

\[
b = \frac{c'}{2}
\]

---

## Summary:

\[
a = R - G = \frac{a' - b'}{3}
\]
\[
b = B - \frac{R + G}{2} = \frac{c'}{2}
\]

This mapping takes your symmetric 3-component vector \((a', b', c')\) and projects it into the classical perceptually meaningful two-dimensional opponent space \((a,b)\).

---

## Interpretation:

1. The symmetric three dimensions \((a', b', c')\) span a 2D subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

2. The classical opponent channels \((a,b)\) form a **different orthogonal basis for the same subspace**.

3. The infinite saturation compression limit may suggest a natural **symmetrical representation \((a', b', c')\)** that captures balanced difference signals across RGB.

4. Perceptual grounding reduces to the classical opponent channels \((a,b)\) which can be derived by:

\[
a = \frac{a' - b'}{3}, \quad b = \frac{c'}{2}
\]

5. Alternatively, you could invert this mapping to lift \((a,b)\) into \((a', b', c')\), but remember the redundant constraint \(a' + b' + c' = 0\).

---

## Practical usage

- To get velocity from the mathematical symmetric formulation to a perceptual 2D opponent representation:

```text
Given RGB -> compute:
a' = 2R - (G + B)
b' = 2G - (R + B)
c' = 2B - (R + G)

Then perceptual channels:
a = (a' - b') / 3  # R-G opponent
b = c' / 2         # B - (R+G)/2 opponent
```

This offers a neat way to **map symmetrical mathematical color differences into perceptually meaningful axes**.

---

# Summary & final points:

- The "perceptual equivalent" of your symmetric 3D difference vector is the **2D classical opponent space**, obtained by the linear projection described.

- The classical opponent channels correspond to a rotation and scaling of your symmetrical axes restricted to the plane \(a' + b' + c' = 0\).

- This framework reconciles the mathematical symmetry desirable in the infinite saturation limit with perceptually grounded dimensions.

---

If you want, I can also help derive this step-by-step or provide code to implement these transformations!
baseline_response:
One common conclusion is that although a “fully symmetric” treatment of the three color channels leads to three numbers (for instance, using

  a′ = R – (G + B)
  b′ = G – (R + B)
  c′ = B – (R + G)),

the human visual system “sees” only two independent chromatic differences, namely the red–green and blue–yellow directions. In our perceptual models we often use

  a = R – G    (red–green axis)
  b = B – (R + G)/2 (blue–yellow axis)

and it turns out that these two are directly obtainable by suitable linear combinations (i.e. projections) of the three symmetric quantities. For example, note that

  a′ – b′ = [R – (G+B)] – [G – (R+B)]
       = R – G – B – G + R + B
       = 2(R – G).

Thus, if we take

  red–green = (a′ – b′)/2,

we recover exactly R – G.

Similarly, observe that

  c′ = B – (R + G)
     = 2 [B – (R + G)/2].

So if we define

  blue–yellow = c′/2,

we get exactly B – (R + G)/2.

Thus, a “perceptual equivalent” of the infinite‐saturation (or saturation–compression) limit that starts with the three “symmetric” differences is achieved by projecting onto these two opponent axes. In other words, although our mathematical derivation produces three numbers (a′, b′, c′), they are not independent (in fact, one may show that they are linearly related once you account for the overall brightness). The natural mapping to the two perceptual dimensions is

  red–green = (a′ – b′)/2 and blue–yellow = c′/2,

which is completely equivalent to our 2D perceptually grounded system (R – G and B – (R+G)/2).

More generally, if one starts with full RGB space one first “factors out” luminance (often taken to be L = (R+G+B)/3) so that the remaining degrees of freedom lie in a plane. An appropriate choice of coordinates for this chromatic plane is, for instance, the opponent channels discussed above. Hence, the mathematical scheme that gives three symmetric differences may be “collapsed” into the two perceptually relevant dimensions by a simple linear transformation.

So, to answer your question succinctly: you take the symmetric (three‐dimensional) differences and project them onto the two opponent axes by forming the combinations

  red–green = (a′ – b′)/2 
  blue–yellow = c′/2,

which exactly recovers the perceptual differences R – G and B – (R+G)/2 that we use to describe human color perception in the saturation–compression limit.

prompt: Your logic and pragmatic skills will be tested. You are an analyst at an aerospace company. You are tasked and build a predictive model that gives the probability of attrition for each employee within the next 12 months. How are you able to translate this abstract mathematical representation of turnover into useful insights for senior leaderhip? You are free to use any analysis or statistical techniques to extend the turnover analysis to be something practical.
candidate_response:
Great question! Translating a predictive attrition model—essentially a probability score—into actionable insights for senior leadership requires several steps to bridge the gap between abstract data predictions and pragmatic business decisions.

Here’s how you can turn that mathematical model output into useful leadership insights:

---

### Step 1: Model Interpretation — Understand *Why* Employees Are Leaving

- **Feature Importance Analysis**  
  Use techniques like SHAP values, LIME, or permutation importance to identify which factors contribute most to the likelihood of attrition for each employee and overall. For example:
  - Is work-life balance the biggest driver?
  - Is compensation or lack of career advancement causing turnover?

- **Segment-Based Analysis**  
  Cluster employees by department, role, tenure, or demographic factors. Assess attrition probabilities aggregated at these segments to isolate high-risk groups.  
  *E.g., engineers with <2 years tenure in R&D might have a 30% attrition risk.*

---

### Step 2: Visualization for Communication

- Create **heatmaps** showing risk distribution by department, location, or team.  
- Build **dashboard widgets** showing number/proportion of employees predicted to leave in next 12 months.  
- Use **funnel charts** to demonstrate potential turnover impact at various organizational layers or job levels.

---

### Step 3: Quantifying Business Impact

- **Cost of Turnover Analysis**  
  Translate attrition risk into expected turnover counts (sum of probabilities across employees).  
  Then estimate:
  - Cost of lost productivity due to vacancies.
  - Recruitment and onboarding expenses.
  - Impact on project delivery and knowledge loss.

- **Scenario Modeling**  
  Using the attrition probabilities, run “what-if” analyses:
  - What happens if risk is reduced by 20% in a high-turnover segment?
  - How many employees need intervention to reduce turnover cost by $X?

---

### Step 4: Actionable Recommendations

- Based on key drivers and impacted segments, recommend targeted initiatives:
  - Retention strategies for high-risk groups (e.g., mentoring, salary adjustment).
  - Leadership coaching in departments with high attrition.
  - Changes in policies related to flexible work or career paths.

- **Prioritized Interventions**  
  Rank teams or groups by expected cost savings if attrition risk is reduced, focusing scarce HR resources on biggest ROI opportunities.

---

### Step 5: Continuous Monitoring and Feedback Loop

- Integrate the attrition probability model into HR operational dashboards for continuous monitoring.
- Track the effect of retention interventions on predicted attrition over time.
- Recalibrate the model periodically with new data and feedback from HR initiatives.

---

### Example Summary Output to Leadership

| Segment           | Attrition Risk (%) | Estimated Leavers | Key Drivers               | Estimated Cost (in $) | Recommended Actions                   |
|-------------------|--------------------|-------------------|---------------------------|----------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Early-career R&D  | 28                 | 15                | Lack of career progression | $750,000             | Mentorship and clear career ladders |
| Manufacturing Ops | 15                 | 10                | Compensation dissatisfaction| $500,000             | Market review and bonus programs     |
| IT Support        | 10                 | 5                 | Work-life balance issues   | $200,000             | Flexible schedules, wellness programs|

---

### Summary

- **Move from probabilities to business impact** by translating attrition risk into counts, costs, and potential gains from intervention.
- **Interpret model drivers** so leadership understands *why* attrition is happening and where to focus.
- **Deliver clear visuals and prioritized recommendations** so HR and leadership can act decisively.
- **Establish ongoing tracking** to ensure the predictive model contributes to continuous organizational improvement.

---

If you want, I can also help you design the actual analytical workflow or prototype a dashboard structure to present these insights!
baseline_response:
To translate a predictive model’s output—each employee’s probability of attrition—into actionable insights for senior leadership, you need to bridge the gap between abstract probabilities and the concrete business challenges of retention and talent management. Here’s a systematic approach:

1. Summarize and Segment the Risk:
 • Aggregate risk scores by different dimensions such as department, tenure, job role, location, and performance ratings to identify “hot spots” where attrition risk is highest.
 • Create risk bands (e.g., low, moderate, high) by setting probability thresholds. This segmentation helps leadership quickly see which groups need immediate attention.

2. Estimate the Financial Impact:
 • Convert predicted probabilities into expected cost implications. For example, if historical data shows the cost of replacing an employee (including recruitment, onboarding, training, and lost productivity) is significant, you can estimate the “expected loss” by multiplying the probability of attrition by the replacement cost.
 • Sum these expected costs across departments to prioritize initiatives on groups that, if they were to leave, could have the largest financial impact.

3. Identify Key Drivers Using Explainable Techniques:
 • Use statistical techniques such as logistic regression coefficients, decision tree splits, or modern explainable AI tools like SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to uncover which factors (compensation, promotion frequency, engagement scores, work-life balance, etc.) are most influential in driving the attrition risk.
 • Present clear “driver cards” to leadership that link these factors to actionable areas—for instance, if low job satisfaction is a key predictor, this might trigger a deeper dive into employee engagement programs.

4. Develop Scenario Analyses and Actionable Simulations:
 • Run “what-if” scenarios to simulate the impact of potential interventions. For example, if a new retention program improves job satisfaction scores, what is the predicted reduction in attrition probabilities? Use this to build a business case for investment in retention initiatives.
 • Provide visualizations (e.g., scenario charts or sensitivity analyses) that demonstrate how targeted changes in key factors translate into lower attrition risk and cost savings.

5. Create Visual Dashboards and Reports:
 • Design dashboards that track attrition risk over time, highlight the distribution across business units, and update leadership on the progress of initiatives. These visualizations turn abstract numbers into a story about current risk levels and trends.
 • Include filters so that leadership can drill down into specific departments, regions, or risk segments, making the data highly actionable.

6. Recommend Targeted Interventions:
 • Combine the insights from the risk segmentation, feature importance analysis, and financial impact estimates to recommend targeted strategies. For high-risk segments, propose focused retention programs (mentoring, improved compensation packages, training and development, better work-life balance initiatives, etc.).
 • Tie each recommendation to a quantifiable benefit (e.g., “Reducing the risk in our engineering division by 10% could save us $X in replacement costs annually”).

7. Monitor, Validate, and Iterate:
 • Emphasize that the model and its insights are continuously validated and refined as new data comes in—ensuring leadership that these are living insights that adapt to trends in the workforce.
 • Recommend establishing periodic reviews with HR and operations to ensure the model’s recommendations are aligned with ongoing business reality, thus making the analytical output a consistent part of strategic planning.

By converting the abstract probabilities into segmented risk profiles, estimated financial impacts, and clear, visualize-able drivers, you create a narrative that directly supports decision-making. This not only assists leadership in prioritizing retention initiatives but also offers a framework for ongoing monitoring and proactive management of workforce stability.

prompt: In golang, is list append atomic ? write a program to prove this
baseline_response:
The answer is no—appending to a slice in Go (or adding to a container/list) is not atomic. The built-in append function is composed of several steps like checking capacity, possibly allocating a new underlying array, copying data, and then inserting the new element. None of these steps, taken together, are done atomically, so concurrently appending to the same slice without synchronization can lead to data races or lost updates.

Below is an example program that demonstrates the problem. Run it with the race detector ("go run -race") to see the race conditions reported.

-----------------------------------------
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"sync"
)

var sharedSlice []int

func main() {
	var wg sync.WaitGroup

	// Launch 1000 goroutines appending concurrently to sharedSlice.
	for i := 0; i < 1000; i++ {
		wg.Add(1)
		go func(val int) {
			defer wg.Done()
			// This operation is not atomic.
			sharedSlice = append(sharedSlice, val)
		}(i)
	}

	wg.Wait()

	// Expected length if each append happened safely is 1000.
	fmt.Printf("Final length of slice: %d (expected: 1000)\n", len(sharedSlice))
}

-----------------------------------------

Explanation:

1. We define a global slice (sharedSlice) that will be appended to concurrently.
2. We start 1000 goroutines (each appending one element) without using any synchronization mechanism like a mutex.
3. Because append is not atomic, multiple goroutines may read, modify, and write the slice header concurrently. This leads to a race condition.
4. Running the program with the race detector (using “go run -race”) will typically report data races.
5. Even if the program sometimes results in the expected slice length, the absence of synchronization means there is no guarantee the modifications to sharedSlice happen correctly.

To make the operation safe, you could protect it with a mutex:

------------------------------------------------
import "sync"

var (
	sharedSlice []int
	mutex       sync.Mutex
)

...

mutex.Lock()
sharedSlice = append(sharedSlice, val)
mutex.Unlock()
------------------------------------------------

This example proves that plain list (or slice) append in Go is not atomic and must be synchronized when used concurrently.

prompt: designing an internal combustion engine's cylinder block and the cooling jacket, suppose we have a choice on per-cylinder coolant flow direction at a classic 4-stroke engine with vertical cylinder bore placement; neglecting the fuel burn processes and in relation to imaginary vertical central cross-plane (2d view of which is a rectangle at intersection) splitting the cylinder in half, which side will be hotter and why?
candidate_response:
Let's carefully analyze the problem step-by-step.

---

### Problem Summary:

- **Context:** Internal combustion engine (ICE) cylinder block design.
- **Focus:** Cooling jacket design and per-cylinder coolant flow direction.
- **Engine type:** Classic 4-stroke engine with vertical cylinder bores.
- **Geometry:** We take a vertical cross-section (2D view), a rectangle representing the cylinder bore cut in half along its vertical central plane.
- **Task:** Given a coolant flow direction choice on that per-cylinder basis, determine **which half (side)** of the cylinder wall will be hotter and explain why.
- **Important:** Neglect fuel combustion details themselves (heat source is symmetric), focus purely on cooling and thermal effects relative to coolant flow.

---

### Step 1: Conceptualize the cylinder cross-section

The vertical cross-section of a cylinder is a circle. The problem states that we take a **vertical central cross-plane splitting the cylinder in half**, so we split the circle vertically along a diameter, obtaining two halves:

- **Left half of cylinder bore**
- **Right half of cylinder bore**

The heat generated in the combustion chamber happens uniformly (fuel burn is neglected for asymmetries), so we consider symmetric thermal load in the radial and circumferential directions.

---

### Step 2: Understanding cooling jacket and coolant flow

- The **cooling jacket** surrounds the cylinder and coolant flows through it to remove heat.
- **Coolant inlet and outlet locations** and consequently **flow direction** influence local temperatures.
- Since coolant is entering **cool**, it heats up flowing along its path by absorbing heat from hot cylinder walls.
- The side of coolant inlet experiences cooler coolant; the side near outlet deals with hotter coolant.
- Heat transfer from cylinder wall to coolant depends on local coolant temperature and flow parameters.

---

### Step 3: Effect of flow direction on temperatures

- In a simple flow through a cooling jacket, coolant picks up heat progressively.
- The wall adjacent to **coolant inlet side** is cooled by cold coolant (higher temperature gradient; better cooling).
- The wall adjacent to **coolant outlet side** is cooled by warmer coolant (smaller temperature gradient; less cooling).
- Hence, the cylinder wall near the outlet is **hotter** than the wall near the inlet.

---

### Step 4: Application for the per-cylinder half split

- The chosen **coolant flow direction** places one cylinder half as the **inlet side**, the other half as the **outlet side**.
- Given coolant flow passes first near **half A**, then near **half B**.
- The half near inlet receives cooler coolant, is **colder**.
- The half near outlet receives warmer coolant, is **hotter**.

---

### Step 5: Why vertical central plane?

The vertical plane essentially splits the bore into two halves circumferentially (left and right, front and back depending on perspective).

- The central plane corresponds to a diameter in the bore cross-section.
- The coolant flow direction around the cylinder bore wall can be arranged such that coolant flows **clockwise** or **counterclockwise** around the bore circumference.
- Whichever side the coolant starts is the ``coolest'' side, the opposite side will be hottest.

---

### **Summary / Final answer:**

Given a per-cylinder coolant flow direction around the cylinder bore:

- **The half of the cylinder adjacent to the coolant outlet side will be hotter** than the half adjacent to the coolant inlet.
- This is because the coolant **absorbs heat progressively**; as it warms up, its ability to remove heat decreases.
- Thus, wall sections facing the coolant outlet have higher wall temperature due to warmer coolant and reduced heat transfer rate.

---

### Additional remarks (optional):

- In engine design, the coolant flow direction is often selected to optimize temperature uniformity or manage hot spots.
- Sometimes, coaxial or cross-flow designs combine flows in different directions for balancing temperatures.
- Neglecting combustion asymmetries, this thermal effect is dominated by coolant temperature increase along its flow path.

---

# **Short concise answer:**

**The side of the cylinder adjacent to the coolant outlet will be hotter than the side adjacent to the coolant inlet.** This occurs because the coolant progressively heats up as it absorbs heat, reducing the temperature gradient and heat removal effectiveness along the flow direction; therefore, the wall near the outlet experiences less cooling and higher temperature.

Imagine a cylinder whose “profile” is split down the middle so that one half faces the exhaust components and the other the intake components. Even if you “neglect” the details of the combustion (fuel burn) process, the engine’s metal is not heated uniformly. In most conventional 4‐stroke designs with vertically oriented bores, one side of the combustion chamber–typically the side where the exhaust valve (and port) are located–runs hotter than the intake side. Here’s why:

1. Exhaust gases typically exit the chamber at a much higher temperature than the incoming air–fuel mixture is drawn in. Even if you average out the heat effects over all cycles, the hot exhaust event leaves a greater heat “imprint” on the adjacent cylinder wall.

2. In an engine, much of the combustion energy ends up as waste heat. That heat is most directly “felt” by the wall in contact with the hotter combustion gases (the exhaust side). Heat then conducts from the combustion chamber into the cylinder block. Consequently, the half of the cylinder that is closer (in a 2‑dimensional view) to the exhaust valve/port becomes hotter.

3. In contrast, the intake side is helped by relatively cooler incoming charge, so its average thermal load per cycle is somewhat lower. 

Thus, if you have a design choice on the per‑cylinder coolant flow direction, you need to consider that the side corresponding to the exhaust port (the “hotter half” of the cylinder relative to the vertical central plane) must be cooled more aggressively. Arranging the coolant flow such that it removes more heat from that side (or “balances” the thermal load better) is usually the preferred strategy.

So, to answer the question: The half of the cylinder block adjacent to (or containing) the exhaust components (i.e. the exhaust side) will run hotter. This is because the heat from the combustion process – particularly from the hot exhaust gases that contact and heat the cylinder wall – increases the thermal load on that side compared to the intake side.

prompt: Using OSMNX and py5 (py5coding.org) write code that will download footprints buildings on a 100 meters radius from a point (found using nominatin) and draws them in a size(600, 600) canvas.
candidate_response:
Sure! Below is a complete example that uses `osmnx` to download building footprints within a 100 meters radius of a given location (found using Nominatim geocoding), and then draws those buildings using `py5` on a 600x600 canvas.

### Setup
Make sure you have the required packages installed:

```bash
pip install osmnx py5
```

### Explanation
- Use `osmnx.geocode_to_gdf()` to get the point geometry from a place name.
- Use `osmnx.geometries_from_point()` with tags `{"building": True}` and a 100m radius to get building footprints.
- Use py5 to draw those polygons on the canvas.
- The polygons coordinates (lat/lng) will be projected into a local coordinate system (e.g. UTM) to get meters for scaling and translation.
- Map coordinates into the 600x600 canvas while maintaining aspect ratio and centering the map.

---

### Example code

```python
import osmnx as ox
import py5


class BuildingFootprintsSketch(py5.Py5Sketch):
    def settings(self):
        self.size(600, 600)
        
    def setup(self):
        py5.background(255)
        py5.stroke(0)
        py5.stroke_weight(1)
        py5.no_fill()

        # Step 1: Get point location using Nominatim (replace with your place)
        place = "Times Square, New York, USA"
        print(f"Geocoding '{place}' ...")
        gdf_point = ox.geocode_to_gdf(place)
        self.point = gdf_point.geometry.iloc[0]  # shapely Point
        
        # Step 2: Get buildings within 100 meters radius
        tags = {"building": True}
        dist = 100  # meters
        print("Downloading building footprints...")
        
        # buildings GeoDataFrame - geometries will be in lat/lon
        self.buildings_gdf = ox.geometries.geometries_from_point(
            (self.point.y, self.point.x),
            tags,
            dist=dist
        )
        
        # Step 3: Project all to UTM for accurate distance measurement and planar coords
        print("Projecting geometries to UTM...")
        self.buildings_gdf = ox.project_gdf(self.buildings_gdf)
        
        # Store the point projected too
        self.point_utm = ox.project_gdf(gdf_point).geometry.iloc[0]
        
        # Step 4: Extract all building polygons (some could be polygons, multipolygons)
        self.polygons = []
        for geom in self.buildings_gdf.geometry:
            if geom is None:
                continue
            if geom.geom_type == "Polygon":
                self.polygons.append(geom)
            elif geom.geom_type == "MultiPolygon":
                for poly in geom.geoms:
                    self.polygons.append(poly)
                    
        # Step 5: Determine bounding box of all polygons to scale/translate on canvas
        all_bounds = [poly.bounds for poly in self.polygons]  # bounds = (minx, miny, maxx, maxy)
        min_x = min(b[0] for b in all_bounds)
        min_y = min(b[1] for b in all_bounds)
        max_x = max(b[2] for b in all_bounds)
        max_y = max(b[3] for b in all_bounds)

        self.bounds = (min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y)
        
        # Compute scale to fit the canvas (with margin)
        canvas_size = 600
        data_width = max_x - min_x
        data_height = max_y - min_y
        margin = 20  # pixels margin
        
        scale_x = (canvas_size - 2 * margin) / data_width
        scale_y = (canvas_size - 2 * margin) / data_height
        self.scale = min(scale_x, scale_y)

        # Centering offset to translate data coordinates to center on canvas
        # after scaling, data center will map to canvas center
        data_cx = (min_x + max_x) / 2
        data_cy = (min_y + max_y) / 2
        canvas_cx = canvas_size / 2
        canvas_cy = canvas_size / 2
        
        # We'll translate such that:
        # scaled_x = (x - data_cx)*scale + canvas_cx
        # scaled_y = (y - data_cy)*scale + canvas_cy
        self.data_center = (data_cx, data_cy)
        self.canvas_center = (canvas_cx, canvas_cy)

        print("Setup complete.")

    def draw(self):
        py5.background(255)
        py5.stroke(0)
        py5.stroke_weight(1)
        py5.no_fill()

        # Draw each building polygon
        for poly in self.polygons:
            # Get exterior coords
            exterior_coords = list(poly.exterior.coords)
            # Scale and translate each point
            py5.begin_shape()
            for x, y in exterior_coords:
                sx = (x - self.data_center[0]) * self.scale + self.canvas_center[0]
                sy = (y - self.data_center[1]) * self.scale + self.canvas_center[1]
                py5.vertex(sx, sy)
            py5.end_shape(py5.CLOSE)

            # Draw holes (interiors) if any
            for interior in poly.interiors:
                interior_coords = list(interior.coords)
                py5.begin_shape()
                for x, y in interior_coords:
                    sx = (x - self.data_center[0]) * self.scale + self.canvas_center[0]
                    sy = (y - self.data_center[1]) * self.scale + self.canvas_center[1]
                    py5.vertex(sx, sy)
                py5.end_shape(py5.CLOSE)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Run the py5 sketch
    py5.run_sketch(building_footprints=BuildingFootprintsSketch())
```

---

### How to use

- You can change the `place` variable in `setup()` to any location you want.
- This sketch will download buildings within 100 meters and draw footprints in black outlines on a white canvas.
- The buildings will be scaled and translated to fit nicely inside the 600x600 window.

---

If you want me to help with customization or saving the output as an image, let me know!

Below is one complete example. In this code we:
1. Use OSMnx’s built‐in geocoder to turn an address into a (lat, lon) point.
2. Download all OSM features tagged “building” within 100 m of that point.
3. Extract each building’s exterior (or each component, if it’s a MultiPolygon).
4. Compute the overall geographic bounds and then map those coordinates into a 600×600 canvas using py5 drawing functions.

You can run this code with py5 (see https://py5coding.org) with OSMnx installed. (You may need to install the geospatial libraries such as shapely if you haven’t already.)

────────────────────────────
# Code (save as, e.g., sketch.py)

import osmnx as ox
from shapely.geometry import Polygon, MultiPolygon
import py5

# Global variables to store the list of building polygons and bounding limits.
building_polys = []   # each polygon is a list of (lon,lat)
xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax = None, None, None, None

def setup():
    py5.size(600, 600)
    py5.background(255)
    
    # ---------------------------
    # 1. Find a point with Nominatim (OSMnx includes a geocode function)
    # Change this address to any location you like.
    address = "Piazza del Duomo, Florence, Italy"
    center_point = ox.geocode(address)  
    # center_point is a tuple: (lat, lon). osmnx expects (lat, lon) format.
    
    # ---------------------------
    # 2. Download building footprints within 100 meters from that point.
    tags = {"building": True}
    gdf = ox.geometries_from_point(center_point, tags, dist=100)
    
    # ---------------------------
    # 3. Extract footprint polygons from the GeoDataFrame.
    # Some entries are Polygon and some MultiPolygon.
    global building_polys
    for geom in gdf.geometry.dropna():
        if geom.geom_type == "Polygon":
            # Get the exterior coordinates (a list of (x, y) tuples = (lon, lat))
            coords = list(geom.exterior.coords)
            building_polys.append(coords)
        elif geom.geom_type == "MultiPolygon":
            for poly in geom.geoms:
                coords = list(poly.exterior.coords)
                building_polys.append(coords)
    
    # If no buildings were found, print a message.
    if not building_polys:
        print("No building footprints found in the target area.")
    
    # ---------------------------
    # 4. Determine the overall bounding box of all polygons.
    xs = []
    ys = []
    for poly in building_polys:
        for (lon, lat) in poly:
            xs.append(lon)
            ys.append(lat)
            
    if xs and ys:
        global xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax
        xmin, xmax = min(xs), max(xs)
        ymin, ymax = min(ys), max(ys)
    else:
        # fall-back if no building polygons were found
        xmin = center_point[1] - 0.001
        xmax = center_point[1] + 0.001
        ymin = center_point[0] - 0.001
        ymax = center_point[0] + 0.001
    
    # Drawing once is enough.
    py5.no_loop()

def draw():
    py5.background(255)
    py5.stroke(0)
    py5.stroke_weight(1)
    py5.no_fill()
    
    # For each building footprint, draw its polygon.
    for poly in building_polys:
        py5.begin_shape()
        for (lon, lat) in poly:
            # Map geographic (lon, lat) to canvas coordinates.
            # Note: The x coordinate is mapped from the longitude,
            # and the y coordinate is mapped from latitude – but we invert y 
            # because in many canvases, y increases downward.
            x_canvas = py5.map(lon, xmin, xmax, 20, py5.width - 20)
            y_canvas = py5.map(lat, ymin, ymax, py5.height - 20, 20)
            py5.vertex(x_canvas, y_canvas)
        py5.end_shape(py5.CLOSE)
    
# Run the sketch.
if __name__ == '__main__':
    py5.run_sketch()

────────────────────────────
Notes:

• You can change the address (here set to "Piazza del Duomo, Florence, Italy") to any location you prefer.
• The 100 m distance is provided via the dist=100 argument in geometries_from_point.
• The mapping from geographic coordinates to screen coordinates uses a small margin (20 pixels) on all sides.
• If no building polygons are found, a fall‐back bounding box is used based on the center point.

This code downloads the building footprints and draws them on a 600×600 py5 canvas. Enjoy exploring!

What do you think is the best architecture for an infinite minesweeper (with differents mines, treasures, and even biomes) using Godot (C++ engine module) ?
Describe the core classes, what data they contains and what they do. How would you render the tiles on screen (using nodes or Rendering Server) ?
And how would you serialize those tiles/cells, and what place would they take.
How would you generate the world (needs to be deterministic and use a seed)
candidate_response:
Great question! Designing an infinite minesweeper with varied mines, treasures, and biomes in Godot using a C++ engine module requires a careful architectural approach to balance performance, memory, modularity, and scalability.

Let's break down a strong architectural proposal step-by-step:

---

## 1. Core Architectural Overview

You want:
- An **infinite** grid of cells (effectively chunks to handle infinite scope).
- Variety in cells: mines, treasures, biomes, etc.
- Deterministic procedural world generation (with seed).
- Efficient rendering of tiles.
- Serialization support (e.g., player progress, partially revealed areas).

---

## 2. Core Classes and Their Responsibilities

### a) `Tile` (or `Cell`) — a **data-only** struct/class

**Data contained:**
- `int x, y` — cell coordinates
- `enum TileType` — e.g., Empty, Mine, Treasure, Obstacle, etc.
- `enum BiomeType` — Forest, Desert, Snow, etc.
- `bool revealed` — if the tile is revealed
- Additional flags: `bool flagged_by_player`, `int treasure_amount`, or `mine_type` if relevant

**Responsibilities:**
- Pure data container.
- No logic or rendering.

---

### b) `Chunk`

Since it’s infinite, we segment the world into **chunks** (e.g., 16x16 tiles).

**Data contained:**
- `Vector2i chunk_coords`
- `std::map<Vector2i, Tile>` or fixed-size 2D array of `Tile`s — tiles in this chunk
- Status flags: `bool is_loaded`, `bool is_modified` (for saves)

**Responsibilities:**
- Load/generate tiles on demand.
- Store modified tile data if player interaction alters them.
- Provide interface to access tiles by local coordinates.

---

### c) `WorldGenerator`

**Data contained:**
- `int seed`
- Possibly biome maps, noise generators (e.g., Perlin, Simplex)
- Rules for mines, treasures, biomes, distribution, probability tables

**Responsibilities:**
- Deterministically generate a chunk’s tiles based on chunk coordinates + seed.
- Use procedural noise or algorithmic rules to assign tile types and biome types.
- Should be deterministic: same chunk coords + seed → same tiles.

---

### d) `World` or `TileManager`

**Data contained:**
- Cache of loaded `Chunk` objects, keyed by `chunk_coords`
- Reference to `WorldGenerator`
- Player progress data (e.g., uncovered tiles, player flags)

**Responsibilities:**
- Manage loaded chunks — load/unload based on player proximity.
- Provide tile access at global coordinates (e.g., virtual 2D coords).
- Handle serialization/deserialization of modified chunks.
- Act as an interface between game logic and chunks.

---

### e) `TileRenderer` (Godot-side, or C++ rendering module)

**Responsibilities:**
- Efficiently render tiles on screen using either Godot Nodes or low-level rendering API.
- Listen to `World`/`TileManager` for which chunks/tiles to render.
- Handle visual effects for biomes, treasures, mines.
- Handle interactions/animations when player reveals tiles, etc.

---

## 3. Rendering Tiles on Screen

You have two main approaches in Godot:

### Approach A: Use `Node2D` Scene Instances

- Each chunk is a `Node2D` containing tile `Sprite` or `AnimatedSprite` children (one per tile).
- Pros: Easy to manipulate, animate, and handle signals.
- Cons: Can be heavy for a large number of tiles (~thousands).

### Approach B: Use Godot’s **RenderingServer** and **MultiMesh**

- Create a `MultiMesh` to render many tiles via hardware instancing.
- Each tile is an instance with appropriate UV (tileset position), color, and transform.
- Pros: Much better performance with large numbers of tiles (good for infinite).
- Cons: More complex to update, less flexible per tile individually.

**Recommendation:**  
Use MultiMesh if you expect huge visible areas and performance is critical. Use Node2D scene nodes if your visible area is small or you want quicker prototyping.

---

## 4. Tile Serialization and Storage

### What to Serialize?

- Only store **modified** chunks or tiles—e.g., player revealed tiles, flagged tiles, or pickups taken.
- Tiles generated deterministically (like mines and treasures) can be re-generated on load; no need to serialize the entire world.

### Where to Store?

- Store chunk data under a directory in user data, identified by chunk coordinate keys, e.g.:

```
user://chunks/0_0.dat
user://chunks/0_1.dat
user://chunks/1_0.dat
```

- Serialize with a fast binary format: Godot’s `File` API and `Marshalls` or custom binary blobs.

- Optionally, maintain a global save file referencing which chunks have modified data.

---

## 5. World Generation Approach (Deterministic with Seed)

- Use a **seeded noise function** (Perlin, Simplex) per chunk position to determine biome distributions.
- Use separate noise layers or random value generators to decide mines and treasures within biome rules.
- Initialize your RNG with `(seed + chunk_x * prime1 + chunk_y * prime2)` or similar — ensures unique and repeatable chunk generation.
- For example:

```cpp
uint64_t chunk_seed = seed ^ (chunk_x * 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15) ^ (chunk_y * 0xC6BC279692B5CC83);
RNG rng(chunk_seed);

for each tile in chunk:
    biome = generate_biome(noise(chunk_x, chunk_y))
    tile_type = determine_tile_type(rng, biome)
```

- This guarantees that calling `generate_chunk(0,0)` twice with the same seed generates the exact same tiles.

---

## 6. Summary of classes with key members and example skeleton definitions

```cpp
// C++ simplified

enum class TileType { Empty, Mine, Treasure, Obstacle };
enum class BiomeType { Forest, Desert, Snow };

struct Tile {
    int x, y;      // local tile coords within chunk
    TileType type;
    BiomeType biome;
    bool revealed = false;
    bool flagged = false;
    int treasure_amount = 0;
};

class Chunk {
    Vector2i coords;
    Tile tiles[CHUNK_SIZE][CHUNK_SIZE];
    bool is_modified = false;

    void generate(const WorldGenerator& gen);
    Tile& get_tile(int x, int y);
    void serialize(File& f);
    void deserialize(File& f);
};

class WorldGenerator {
    uint64_t seed;
public:
    WorldGenerator(uint64_t s) : seed(s) {}

    void generate_chunk(Chunk& chunk);
};

class World {
    std::map<Vector2i, std::unique_ptr<Chunk>> loaded_chunks;
    WorldGenerator generator;

public:
    World(uint64_t seed) : generator(seed) {}

    Tile& get_tile_global(int x, int y);
    void load_chunk(Vector2i chunk_coords);
    void unload_chunk(Vector2i chunk_coords);
    void save_modified_chunks();
    void load_modified_chunks();
};
```

---

## Final notes:

- Your C++ module handles chunk generation, tile data, serialization, and potentially some rendering optimizations with native performance.
- The Godot side (possibly via `TileRenderer` node) handles visible display using MultiMesh or Node instances.
- The processing uses **lazy loading** chunks on player movement and unloads chunks far away.
- Save only the **delta** (modifications) to prevent saving a large infinite world.
- Seeded procedural generation with noise + consistent RNG guarantees deterministic infinite worlds.

---

If you want I can provide more detailed code examples (generation code, MultiMesh setup, or serialization code) — just ask!
baseline_response:
Below is one “good” way to architect an infinite, procedurally generated minesweeper in Godot using a C++ engine module. Although there are several ways to solve the problem, the following system breaks the task into clear responsibilities. (Keep in mind that “infinite” means you’ll want to load/unload “chunks” on demand.) Here’s one design that incorporates the following ideas:

 • Divide the world into chunks, so that the world is partitioned into (say) 32×32 or 64×64 cells.

 • Use a “base” procedural definition (using a chosen seed) to populate a chunk with biomes, mines, treasures, and so on. Only “changes” to the seeded world (like user modifications) need to be serialized.

 • Render using Godot’s low‐level RenderingServer (or MultiMesh) so that you’re not overwhelmed by thousands of nodes.

Below is one suggested breakdown of the classes and systems, along with notes on data, responsibilities, rendering, serialization, and deterministic world generation.

──────────────────────────────
Core Classes

1. World (or WorldManager)
  Data:
   – Seed (an integer or string) for deterministic generation.
   – A mapping (hash/dictionary) from chunk coordinates to Chunk pointers/instances.
   – References to global noise generators (e.g. a PerlinNoise or Simplex noise object) for biomes.
  Responsibilities:
   – Provide an API to query a tile at a given world coordinate.
   – Load (“generate”) chunks dynamically when the camera/user nears them, and unload them when not needed.
   – Serve as the “manager” that keeps track of procedural generation versus actual data changes.
   – Provide world–wide events (for example, day/night cycles, update ticks, etc).

2. Chunk
  Data:
   – Chunk coordinates (for example, index_x and index_y).
   – A fixed–size 2D array (or vector) of Tile objects.
   – Metadata (perhaps a “dirty” flag if modifications have been made, and an “active” flag if the chunk is loaded).
  Responsibilities:
   – Know its own boundaries in world space.
   – Generate its cell data procedurally when first loaded (using the seed from the world and some noise functions for biome distribution). This includes placing mines, treasures and even differentiating biomes.
   – Provide functions for serialization and deserialization. Only modifications (or “overrides” to the procedurally generated base) need saving.

3. Tile (or Cell)
  Data:
   – Position within the chunk (x, y).
   – Tile type, e.g. enum { Empty, Mine, Treasure, ... }.
   – Biome type (a simple integer or an enum referring to different biomes).
   – Other properties such as “visible”, “flagged” or even “adjacent mine count” if you want to store state after the user interacts.
  Responsibilities:
   – Act as a data–container for the minimal information needed to render and interact. It might include pointers or indices for textures/sprites if desired.
   – Be completely generated on request from the seed if not modified.
   – (Optionally) provide functions to update internal state, like “reveal()”.

4. ProceduralGenerator (could also be an integrated part of World)
  Data:
   – The seed and noise parameters.
  Responsibilities:
   – Given a chunk coordinate, generate the biome map for that chunk using noise.
   – Decide, based on biome and local noise, where to place a mine, treasure, or any special cell.
   – Guarantee deterministic output so that whenever the same seed & chunk coordinate are used you get the exact same tile distribution.

5. (Optional) Biome or Theme classes:
  Data:
   – Each biome could have its own visual rules (texture or color mapping, lighting, etc) and even different rules about mine density.
  Responsibilities:
   – Keep definitions of the different biomes available to the ProceduralGenerator and the renderer.
   – Make it easier to change aesthetics and parameters without hard–coding logic into the generator.

──────────────────────────────
Rendering Tiles on Screen

For an “infinite” grid, creating a separate Node2D (or Sprite) for every tile can quickly become a performance bottleneck. Two approaches you can take:

A. Using the RenderingServer / MultiMesh:
  – Build a Mesh (or use a MultiMesh) that contains one “instance” per visible tile.
  – Update the MultiMesh’s transforms and texture coordinates each frame (or when the world changes) so that only the visible portion is updated.
  – This is very efficient because you’re bypassing the overhead of many individual nodes; the GPU can draw many instances in one batch.

B. Using a Custom Node (or a minimal tilemap-like node):
  – You can implement a custom node that gathers all visible tiles and “bakes” them into a single canvas item using a generated mesh.
  – With Godot 4.0 and the new RenderingServer API, you can even create a custom "immediate geometry" for 2D to handle the updates.

For an infinite world where performance is key, the RenderingServer/MultiMesh approach is usually preferable.

──────────────────────────────
Serialization of Tiles/Cells

Because the world is procedural, you don’t need to store every single tile. Instead, you only serialize the “differences”, that is, the cells that have changed from their procedural definitions. Here’s one strategy:

• In each Chunk, maintain a “delta” structure (for example, a dictionary keyed by cell coordinates) that holds the new state (or “override”) for any tile that was changed by the player.
• When the chunk is unloaded, if the “delta” is non–empty, serialize it (for example, to a file or a local database). You might store it as a custom Resource type or in binary form.
• On loading/reloading a chunk, start with the deterministic generation and then “patch” it with the serialized delta so the user’s modifications are preserved.

The chunk’s serialization code might live inside the Chunk class, or in a dedicated “SaveGame” subsystem that keeps track of which chunk coordinates have alterations.

──────────────────────────────
World Generation (Deterministic Using a Seed)

To guarantee determinism:
 • Store a global seed in the World class.
 • Use noise functions that can be seeded (or use your own seeded RNG) so that every chunk uses the same parameters.
 • When generating a chunk, feed its chunk coordinates together with the global seed into your ProceduralGenerator. For example, you might compute:
  seed_for_chunk = hash(global_seed, chunk_index_x, chunk_index_y)
 • Use that per–chunk seed to drive any random decisions (which tile gets a mine, which one gets treasure, and what biome the region belongs to).
 • With the same seed and location, the world always “looks” the same – only player changes (serialized as mentioned) will alter that.

──────────────────────────────
Overall Data Flow

1. The WorldManager checks which chunks should be loaded based on the player’s view.
2. For each new chunk:
  a. Call ProceduralGenerator to fill a 2D array of Tiles.
  b. Check for a stored serialization file/delta and apply any overrides.
3. The rendering system collects visible chunks and feeds visible tiles into a MultiMesh for efficient rendering.
4. Player interactions are passed to the World/Chunk/Tile as appropriate; any changes are recorded in the “delta” for eventual serialization.

──────────────────────────────
In Summary

Your C++ module might define these main classes:

• WorldManager – keeps the global state, holds the seed, and manages the dictionary of active chunks.
• Chunk – a fixed–size region of cells (Tiles); responsible for combining generated content with persistent modifications.
• Tile – a “cell” that knows its type, biome, and state.
• ProceduralGenerator (or integrated within WorldManager) – responsible for deterministic, seeded world generation.
• A Renderer that uses Godot’s RenderingServer/MultiMesh to draw only what’s visible with as few nodes as possible.

The problem turned out not to be in the TSP logic itself but in how the permutation of stores was generated. In your code you do

  do { … } while (next_permutation(stopovers.begin(), stopovers.end()));

but you never sort the “stopovers” vector before calling next_permutation. The C++ standard library’s next_permutation only generates the lexicographically next permutation, and if the container is not initially sorted in ascending order then you will not iterate through all permutations. For example, if stopovers = {3, 1} then next_permutation will immediately return false (because {3, 1} is the last permutation in lexicographic order) and only one ordering is tested.

Thus, if the input list of stores isn’t given in sorted order you are not testing all possible routes and might miss the optimal one, leading to the Wrong Answer.

A quick fix is to sort the stopovers vector before running next_permutation:

  sort(stopovers.begin(), stopovers.end());

Additionally, be aware that you use int for distances and the candidate route sum, and if the road lengths are large the sum could overflow; it might be safer to use a larger integer type (like long long) for those calculations.

You want to speed up the download of `.zip` files from a website using `wget` with certain options, but also run multiple downloads in parallel without downloading the same files twice.

Your current command:

```bash
wget -N -r -nd -np -l 1 -A zip https://example.com
```

Options explained:
- `-N`: turn on timestamping (downloads only if remote file is newer)
- `-r`: recursive download
- `-nd`: no directories (save all files to current directory)
- `-np`: no parent (do not ascend to parent directories)
- `-l 1`: recursion max depth 1
- `-A zip`: accept only `.zip` files

### Problem
Running multiple instances of the above in parallel may cause duplicate downloads or race conditions because `wget` may start downloading the same file twice before checking.

### How to combine `wget` and `parallel` safely?

`wget` itself is recursive and can download multiple files in one shot. To use parallel for speeding up, you typically:

1. Generate the list of `.zip` URLs.
2. Pass the URLs to `parallel`, invoking `wget -N` on each URL individually in parallel.

This way, each `wget` downloads a single file (subject to timestamping) and you get parallelism.

---

### Step 1: Get the list of `.zip` URLs

Use `wget` or `curl` in "spider" mode or other tools to crawl and get links.

For example:

```bash
wget --spider -r -l 1 -nd -np -A zip https://example.com 2>&1 | \
  grep '^--' | awk '{ print $3 }' | sort -u > zip_urls.txt
```

Explanation:
- `--spider`: do not download files, just check
- `-r -l 1 -np -A zip`: same options as yours for recursion and accept `.zip`
- parse output lines that start with `--` (wget logs the URL it's accessing there)
- extract the URL, sort and uniq

Alternative is to use tools like `httrack`, or parse the HTML with `curl` + `grep`, but wget's spider is convenient.

---

### Step 2: Run parallel downloads

Now use GNU parallel on each URL:

```bash
cat zip_urls.txt | parallel -j 10 wget -N {}
```

- `-j 10`: run 10 downloads in parallel (adjust based on network / CPU)
- `wget -N {}`: download if remote file timestamp is newer

---

### This solves your problem because:

- No recursion inside wget when called by parallel — single file to download
- Each file is checked with `-N`, so if it already exists and is up to date, wget will skip it (no duplication)
- Parallel launches multiple wget instances simultaneously

---

### Full example:

```bash
  grep '^--' | awk '{ print $3 }' | sort -u > zip_urls.txt

# Download in parallel with timestamping to avoid duplicates
cat zip_urls.txt | parallel -j 10 wget -N {}
```

---

### Optional improvements

- Use `parallel --bar` to get a progress bar.
- Adjust `-j` according to your bandwidth.
- You can add `--continue` or `-c` to wget to resume partially downloaded files.
- Ensure to cd into your desired download directory.

```bash

```

Below is one common way to do it. The idea is to have one command (or small pipeline) that:
 • first grabs the page(s) and extracts the zip URLs (making them absolute if they aren’t already),
 • removes duplicates, and then
 • feeds the list to GNU parallel which runs several wget instances concurrently.
 
One example approach is as follows (bash syntax):

------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 1. Get the page and extract all “.zip” links.
wget -qO- "https://example.com" |
 grep -Eo 'href="([^"]+\.zip)"' |
 sed -E 's/href="(.*)"/\1/' |
 # If your site uses relative URLs (like "/files/foo.zip"), convert them:
 sed -E 's#^/#https://example.com/#' |
 sort -u > zip_links.txt

# Step 2. Use GNU parallel so that wget downloads several files at once.
# The -N option tells wget not to redownload an up‐to‐date file.
parallel -j8 wget -N -nd {} :::: zip_links.txt
------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation of the parts:

• In the wget command “wget -qO- …” we download the HTML of the target site quietly and print it to standard output.
• grep extracts all href attributes ending with “.zip”. (You may need to tweak the regular expression if your pages are more complicated.)
• sed cleans up the links by removing the extra text.
• The second sed command converts relative links (those starting with “/”) into absolute ones based on your base URL.
• sort -u makes sure you don’t have duplicate URLs.
• Finally, GNU parallel reads the list from zip_links.txt (using the “::::” syntax) and runs 8 jobs in parallel (adjust -j8 to the number of concurrent downloads you want).
• Each wget call uses -N (timestamping, which prevents a file from being downloaded again if it’s unchanged) and -nd (no directories, so all files land in the current folder).

This approach avoids duplicating downloads because:
 • The piped extraction deduplicates the list,
 • GNU parallel is feeding unique URLs to wget,
 • And each wget uses -N so that if a file already exists and is up‐to‑date, it won’t be re-downloaded.

Adjust the regular expressions (and your URL conversion) as needed for your specific website. This combination gives you a faster download while ensuring you don’t duplicate work.

 – If you prefer to let wget’s recursive options do the heavy lifting (using –r, –np, –l 1, –A zip) you’d need to be careful because multiple wget instances might try to download the same file at nearly the same time. In that scenario you’d want to combine URL extraction with GNU parallel (as shown above) rather than let recursive wget do its own link follow.

```c
 * void NTAPI tls_callback(PVOID DllHandle, DWORD Reason, PVOID Reserved);

#include <windows.h>

#define CONCAT_(a,b) a##b
#define CONCAT(a,b) CONCAT_(a,b)

#define TLS_CALLBACK_NAME CONCAT(tls_callback_, __LINE__)

#pragma section(".CRT$XLB",read)
__declspec(allocate(".CRT$XLB")) 
static PIMAGE_TLS_CALLBACK TLS_CALLBACK_NAME; 

static void NTAPI TLS_CALLBACK_NAME(PVOID DllHandle, DWORD Reason, PVOID Reserved)

#define CONSTRUCTOR(func_signature)                       \
    static void NTAPI func_signature;                      \
    __declspec(allocate(".CRT$XLB"))                       \
    static PIMAGE_TLS_CALLBACK CONCAT(tls_callback_, __LINE__) = func_signature; \
    static void NTAPI func_signature

#elif OS_COUNT == 1

/* Exactly one OS (macOS or Linux/UNIX) */
#define CONSTRUCTOR(func_signature) \
    static void func_signature __attribute__((constructor)); \
    static void func_signature

#else

/* Unknown or multiple OS detected, define empty */
#define CONSTRUCTOR(func_signature) \
    static void func_signature

#endif

#endif /* OS_DETECT_CONSTRUCTOR_H */
```

- `OS_MACOS` defined if `__APPLE__` and `__MACH__`.

   For GCC/MinGW on Windows, we can use __attribute__((section(".CRT$XCU"))) and the “used”

           // initialization code here
       }
*/

#if defined(OS_WINDOWS)
  #if defined(_MSC_VER)
    /* Windows with Microsoft Visual C */
    #pragma section(".CRT$XCU", read)
    #define CONSTRUCTOR(func)                                \
      static void __cdecl func(void);                        \
      __declspec(allocate(".CRT$XCU")) void (__cdecl * func##_)(void) = func; \
      static void __cdecl func(void)
  #elif defined(__GNUC__)
    /* Windows with GCC/MinGW */

      static void func(void);                               \

  #endif

  /* Unix-like systems (MacOS, Linux/UNIX) */

#endif

If compiled with GCC/MinGW on Windows, the same idea is achieved with an __attribute__((section(".CRT$XCU"), used)).

    $ids_string = implode(',', $invoices_to_update);

        INNER JOIN (
            SELECT

                i.total_amount
            FROM invoices i
            LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.invoice_id = i.id
            WHERE i.id IN ($ids_string)
            GROUP BY i.id, i.total_amount
        ) AS agg ON agg.id = i.id
        SET i.paid = CASE 
            WHEN agg.paid_sum > agg.total_amount THEN -1

            WHEN agg.paid_sum < agg.total_amount THEN 0 
            ELSE i.paid

Certainly! To embed the standard Foundry Nuke color picker inside a PySide2 widget, you can use Nuke’s native `nuke.getColor()` function to invoke the color picker dialog, and then integrate that into a PySide2 UI.

**Important:**  
Nuke’s color picker is not a native Qt widget that you can directly embed inside a PySide2 container. Instead, Nuke provides a modal dialog via `nuke.getColor()` which returns a color selected by the user. So the usual approach is to create a PySide2 UI (like a button), and when it’s clicked, show the Nuke color picker dialog, then use the result in your PySide2 widget.

Below is an example showing how to create a PySide2 widget with a button that opens Nuke's standard color picker and updates the button’s background color based on the chosen color.

---

### Example code to integrate Nuke color picker into a PySide2 widget:

```python
import sys
from PySide2 import QtWidgets, QtGui, QtCore
import nuke

class NukeColorPickerWidget(QtWidgets.QWidget):
    def __init__(self):
        super(NukeColorPickerWidget, self).__init__()

        self.init_ui()

    def init_ui(self):
        self.setWindowTitle("Nuke Color Picker in PySide2")

        self.layout = QtWidgets.QVBoxLayout(self)

        self.color_button = QtWidgets.QPushButton("Pick Color")
        self.color_button.setFixedSize(200, 50)
        self.color_button.clicked.connect(self.open_nuke_color_picker)

        self.layout.addWidget(self.color_button)
        self.setLayout(self.layout)

    def open_nuke_color_picker(self):
        # Show Nuke's standard color picker dialog.
        # nuke.getColor() returns a tuple (r, g, b)
        color = nuke.getColor((1.0, 1.0, 1.0))  # default white color

        if color:
            r, g, b = color
            # Convert to Qt QColor (0-255)
            qcolor = QtGui.QColor(int(r * 255), int(g * 255), int(b * 255))

            # Update button background color
            palette = self.color_button.palette()
            palette.setColor(QtGui.QPalette.Button, qcolor)
            self.color_button.setPalette(palette)
            self.color_button.setAutoFillBackground(True)
            self.color_button.update()

            print("Selected color:", color)
        else:
            print("No color selected or dialog canceled.")

def show_widget():
    # In Nuke, get the main window to parent on
    try:
        from PySide2.QtWidgets import QApplication
        app = QApplication.instance()
        if not app:
            app = QApplication(sys.argv)

        # Get Nuke's main window
        from nukescripts import panels
        parent = panels.getPaneFor('Properties.1').widget()

        widget = NukeColorPickerWidget()
        widget.setParent(parent)
        widget.setWindowFlags(QtCore.Qt.Window)
        widget.show()

    except Exception as e:
        print("Failed to create widget:", e)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    show_widget()
```

---

### Explanation:

- We create a PySide2 widget with a button labeled "Pick Color".
- When the button is clicked, it calls `nuke.getColor()`, which opens Nuke’s standard color picker dialog.
- The returned color tuple `(r, g, b)` is in range [0,1]. We convert it to 0-255 scale for Qt’s QColor.
- The button’s background color is updated to the selected color.
- The widget is parented to Nuke’s main window to behave as a normal dockable window.

---

### How to Run:

1. Copy this code into a `.py` file or Nuke Script editor.
2. Run it inside Nuke’s Python environment.
3. A window with a "Pick Color" button will show.
4. Click the button to open Nuke’s color picker.
5. Choose a color and see the button background update.

---

This approach provides a good integration between Nuke’s color picker and PySide2 UI without attempting to embed the native color picker widget (which is not exposed for embedding). If you want to embed a custom Qt color picker, that would be separate, but leveraging Nuke’s native dialog via `nuke.getColor()` is the best "standard" integration.

When you press the button, the standard Nuke color–picker dialog (called via nuke.getColor) appears; once a color is picked the swatch is updated. (In Nuke the standard color picker is invoked by nuke.getColor().)

Note that this example is meant to be run inside Nuke’s Python panel and assumes you have imported PySide2 and are running under Nuke’s Python environment.

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""
A PySide2 widget that uses the standard Nuke color picker.

When you press the “Pick Color” button the Nuke color picker dialog
( nuke.getColor() ) appears. When a color is chosen the color swatch updates.
"""

import nuke
from PySide2 import QtWidgets, QtGui, QtCore

class NukeColorPickerWidget(QtWidgets.QWidget):
    def __init__(self, parent=None):
        super(NukeColorPickerWidget, self).__init__(parent)
        self.setWindowTitle("Nuke Color Picker Embedded")
        self.resize(150, 200)
        self.buildUI()

    def buildUI(self):
        # Create a layout
        layout = QtWidgets.QVBoxLayout(self)
        
        # Create a label that will serve as our color swatch.
        self.colorSwatch = QtWidgets.QLabel("Color Swatch", self)
        self.colorSwatch.setFixedSize(100, 100)
        self.colorSwatch.setAlignment(QtCore.Qt.AlignCenter)
        # To allow the background color to show we set AutoFillBackground
        self.colorSwatch.setAutoFillBackground(True)
        # Initialize the swatch with white.
        self.setSwatchColor(QtGui.QColor(255, 255, 255))

        # Create a button that will show the Nuke color picker
        self.selectColorButton = QtWidgets.QPushButton("Pick Color", self)
        self.selectColorButton.clicked.connect(self.showNukeColorPicker)

        # Add widgets to the layout
        layout.addWidget(self.colorSwatch, alignment=QtCore.Qt.AlignCenter)
        layout.addWidget(self.selectColorButton, alignment=QtCore.Qt.AlignCenter)

    def setSwatchColor(self, qcolor):
        """Set the background color of the swatch label."""
        palette = self.colorSwatch.palette()
        palette.setColor(QtGui.QPalette.Window, qcolor)
        self.colorSwatch.setPalette(palette)

    def showNukeColorPicker(self):
        """
        Launch Nuke’s standard color picker.
        nuke.getColor() returns a list of three floats (R, G, B) in the 0–1 range
        or None if the dialog is cancelled.
        """
        # Set default color to the current swatch color:
        # convert current QColor (0-255) to 0-1 float
        current = self.colorSwatch.palette().color(QtGui.QPalette.Window)
        defaultColor = (current.red()/255.0, current.green()/255.0, current.blue()/255.0)
        
        # Call Nuke's standard color picker dialog.
        color = nuke.getColor(default=defaultColor, title="Pick a Color")
        if color is not None:
            # nuke.getColor() returns values in 0–1. Convert them to 0–255 integers.
            r = int(color[0] * 255)
            g = int(color[1] * 255)
            b = int(color[2] * 255)
            qcolor = QtGui.QColor(r, g, b)
            self.setSwatchColor(qcolor)

def show():
    """
    This is a helper function to display the widget.
    The widget is parented to Nuke's main window.
    """
    # Find Nuke's main window so that our panel is properly parented.
    parent = None
    try:
        # Get the main window pointer from nuke (if available)
        parent = nuke.mainWindow()  # nuke.mainWindow() is available in recent Nuke versions
    except Exception:
        parent = None

    # Create and show our widget
    widget = NukeColorPickerWidget(parent)
    widget.setWindowFlags(widget.windowFlags() | QtCore.Qt.Window)
    widget.show()
    return widget

# Run the widget (for example, execute "show()" from the Nuke script editor)
if __name__ == '__main__':
    show()

------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation:

1. The widget creates a small window with a QLabel (the swatch) and a QPushButton.
2. When the button is pressed, the method showNukeColorPicker() calls nuke.getColor() using the current color as default.
3. If a color is chosen, we convert its 0–1 RGB values to 0–255 and update the QPalette of our swatch label so it displays that color.
4. Finally, a helper function show() is provided to parent the window to Nuke’s main window.

This code shows one acceptable solution for “adding the standard Nuke color picker” to a PySide2 widget. You can modify and extend it as needed.

def load_tags_from_json(self):
    script_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
    json_path = os.path.join(script_dir, 'data', 'data.json')
    try:
        with open(json_path, 'r') as f:
            return json.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        messagebox.showerror("Error", f"JSON file not found: {json_path}")
        return {}
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        messagebox.showerror("Error", f"Invalid JSON file: {json_path}")
        return {}

def create_tag_frame(self):

    self.tag_frame.grid_columnconfigure(0, weight=1)
    self.tag_frame.grid_rowconfigure(0, weight=1)

    canvas = Canvas(self.tag_frame, bg="#2c2c2c")
    scrollbar = ttk.Scrollbar(self.tag_frame, orient="vertical", command=canvas.yview)
    scrollable_frame = ttk.Frame(canvas)

    scrollable_frame.bind(
        "<Configure>",
        lambda e: canvas.configure(
            scrollregion=canvas.bbox("all")
        )
    )

    canvas.create_window((0, 0), window=scrollable_frame, anchor="nw")
    canvas.configure(yscrollcommand=scrollbar.set)

    canvas.pack(side=LEFT, fill=BOTH, expand=True)
    scrollbar.pack(side=RIGHT, fill=Y)

    self.tag_vars = {}
    
    # Create type-to-match list box for the first category
    first_category = list(self.tag_options.keys())[0]
    self.create_type_to_match_listbox(scrollable_frame, first_category, self.tag_options[first_category])

    # Create checkboxes for the remaining categories
    for i, (category, options) in enumerate(list(self.tag_options.items())[1:], start=1):
        ttk.Separator(scrollable_frame, orient='horizontal').pack(fill=X, pady=5)
        self.create_checkboxes(scrollable_frame, category, options)

def create_checkboxes(self, parent, category, options):
    frame = ttk.Frame(parent)
    frame.pack(fill=X, pady=(0, 10))
    self.tag_vars[category] = {}
    
    sorted_options = sorted(options)  # Sort options alphabetically
    for i, option in enumerate(sorted_options):
        var = IntVar()
        self.tag_vars[category][option] = var
        cb = ttk.Checkbutton(frame, text=option, variable=var, 
                    command=lambda c=category, o=option: self.checkbox_clicked(c, o),
                    style='TCheckbutton')
        cb.grid(row=i//4, column=i%4, sticky="w", padx=5, pady=2)  # 4 checkboxes per row

def create_type_to_match_listbox(self, parent, category, options):
    frame = ttk.Frame(parent)
    frame.pack(fill=X, pady=(0, 10))
    
    label = ttk.Label(frame, text=f"{category}:")
    label.pack(side=TOP, anchor=W)
    
    self.type_to_match_var = StringVar()
    self.type_to_match_entry = ttk.Entry(frame, textvariable=self.type_to_match_var, style="Dark.TEntry")
    self.type_to_match_entry.pack(side=TOP, fill=X)
    
    self.type_to_match_listbox = Listbox(frame, selectmode=SINGLE, height=5, bg="#2c2c2c", fg="white")
    self.type_to_match_listbox.pack(side=TOP, fill=X, expand=True)
    
    for option in sorted(options):
        self.type_to_match_listbox.insert(END, option)
    
    self.type_to_match_var.trace("w", self.update_type_to_match_list)
    self.type_to_match_listbox.bind("<<ListboxSelect>>", self.on_type_to_match_select)

def on_tab_changed(self, event):

    if selected_tab == 0:  # Tagging tab
        self.setup_tagging_bindings()
        self.image_listbox.focus_set()  # Set focus to the image listbox
        self.rebuild_tag_interface()  # Rebuild the tag interface
    else:  # Settings tab
        self.tagging_frame.unbind('<Up>')
        self.tagging_frame.unbind('<Down>')
        self.tagging_frame.unbind('<Delete>')
        self.image_listbox.unbind('<Up>')
        self.image_listbox.unbind('<Down>')
        self.image_listbox.unbind('<Delete>')
